events.event_narrative: The first measurable precipitation in 57 days fell on the first of the month. However, the measured precipitation was only a few hundredths of an inch of melted snow. This was not enough to keep the county from entirely slipping into extreme drought (D3) by the 4th.   The county spent the rest of the month in extreme drought as the month ended with only a precipitation total of one tenth of an inch of liquid. The county still remained in a 6 to 12 inch deficit over the previous 12 months.

With an 80-85 day stretch of zero measurable precipitation through November and December, the streak ended with areas receiving a couple hundredths of an inch of liquid. This was what some light snow melted down to on the first of the month. Another snow event brought some very dry snow to the county on the 20th as well. With 1.5 to 2 inches of snow that only melted down to a few hundredths of an inch of liquid. Given this, D4 Exceptional Drought levels emerged in January for most of the county.

With an 50-85 day stretch of zero measurable precipitation through November and December, the streak ended with areas receiving a couple hundredths of an inch of liquid. This was what some light snow melted down to on the first of the month. Another snow event brought some very dry snow to the county on the 20th as well. With 1.5 to 2 inches of snow that only melted down to a few hundredths of an inch of liquid, the Extreme Drought (D3) continued to expand east and some Exceptional (D4) drought emerged in western portions of the county.

Dallam County entered the month of January with the majority of the extreme drought (D3), with the exception of the far southwest corner of the county was in severe drought (D2). By mid month the area of severe drought slipped into extreme drought.  Dallam County went 79 to 80 days straight without precipitation going into the month of January. This streak of no measurable precipitation ended on the first. However, the month only ended with a few hundredths of an inch of liquid which was not enough to improve already dire conditions. The county still remained in a  4 to 8 inch deficit over the previous 12 months.

Sherman County went 79 to 80 days straight without measurable precipitation leading into January.  Some snow fell ending this pattern of no precipitation during the month. However, it was not enough to end the extreme drought (D3) conditions being experienced across the entire county. The little bit of precipitation that was received during the month was only enough to keep conditions from slipping into exceptional drought (D4). The previous 12 month provided a 2 to 6 inch rainfall deficit and very dry soil.

Hansford County went close to 60 days without seeing any measurable precipitation prior to January. With the county already being in extreme drought (D3) conditions did not improve during the month as the precipitation that did fall during the month only amounted to around 0.08 to 0.10 inches for a monthly total. The extreme drought continued through the end of the month with a 4 to 6 inch deficit in the last 180 days.

The county went close to 60 days straight with no measurable precipitation leading into the month of January. Although this streak ended, precipitation remained below average. Only about half of the southwestern portion of the county was in extreme drought (D3), with the other half in sever drought (D2), at the end of December.  Going into the month of January the entire county succumbed to extreme drought within the first week. Some very dry snow fell in during the month. However, this was not enough to improve conditions, only hold back further deterioration.   Ochiltree County remained in a 2 to 6 deficit over the previous 180 days.

Lipscomb County ended December with close to 60 days straight with no precipitation and the entire county in severe drought (D2). Though some precipitation fell on the first of January, it was not enough to prevent the county from slipping into extreme drought (D3) the during the first few days of January. The county remained in D3 through the entire month as the monthly total precipitation was only around a tenth of an inch, and the county remained in a 2 to 6 inch deficit over the previous 180 days.

Hartley County ended December with close to 80 days straight with no measurable precipitation, and the southwest half of the county was in severe drought (D2), while the northeast half was in extreme drought (D3). The first of January brought some measurable precipitation but totals remained below normal which led to degradation to extreme D3 within the first week of January.  Less than a tenth of an inch of liquid fell during the whole month and the county remained in a 2 to 6 inch deficit over the previous 180 days.

Moore County went into January with widespread extreme drought (D3) conditions across the entire county. Some moisture fell during the month but only enough to keep the status quo. The county ended the month still in extreme drought. The area stayed in a  2 to 6 inch deficit over the previous 180 days.

Hutchinson County went into January with widespread extreme drought (D3) conditions across the entire county. Some moisture fell during the month but only enough to keep the status quo. The county ended the month still in extreme drought with a 2 to 6 inch deficit over the previous 180 days.

Roberts County went into January with widespread extreme drought (D3) conditions across the entire county. Some moisture fell during the month but only enough to keep the status quo. The county ended the month still in extreme drought with a 4 to 8 inch deficit over the past 180 days.

With most of the county in extreme drought (D3) going into the month of January, the western third remained in severe drought (D2) through about the 3rd week before falling into extreme drought with the rest of the county. A 2 to 6 inch rainfall deficit was experienced over the previous 180 days.

A little over half of Randall County was in extreme drought (D3) going into the month of January, while the rest of the eastern portion of the county stayed in severe drought (D2) only for a the first few days of the month. This area of D2 slipped into extreme drought during the first few days and stayed there with with rest of the county through the end of January as the county remained in a 2 to 6 inch deficit over the previous 180 days.

Armstrong County went into the month of January with severe drought conditions (D2).  Within the first few days the north to northwest two thirds of the county slipped into extreme drought (D3).  The county remained this way through the rest of the month given a 2 to 6 inch rainfall deficit over the previous 180 days.

Collingsworth County went into the month of January with the northeast half of the county in extreme drought (D3). Within the first few days of the month the rest of the county that was in severe drought (D2) slipped into extreme drought as well and stayed through the end of the month. The county ended the month in a 4 to 8 inch deficit over the past 180 days.

Donley County went into the month of January with severe drought conditions (D2).  Within the first few days the north to northeast three fourths of the county slipped into extreme drought (D3) given a 4 to 8 inch rainfall deficit over the past 180 days.

The Carbon Camp fire began 1 mile southeast of Stinnett, Texas in Hutchinson County. The Carbon Camp fire began just south of Carbon Camp Road and spread south towards the Scotts Acres subdivision. Evacuations were in place for the residents of Scotts Acres subdivision in Stinnett, Texas. State Highway 136 was shut down for a period of time. There was a report of as many as 85 structures threatened. Three structures or properties, one occupied home, one barn and an RV, were lost. However, there were no reports of any injuries or fatalities. The fire consumed 177 acres and was contained as of 1300CST on January 15, 2022. Multiple local fire departments from Stinnett VFD, Crutch VFD, Fritch VFD, Borger FD, Potter County FD, Skellytown VFD, responded to assist along with National Parks Service (NPS), Pantex and State resources from the Texas A&M Forest Service (TAMFS). TAMFS and Stinnett Fire Department worked in unified command. Aircraft was ordered but canceled.

OFS Suppression Group assisted multiple Beaver County Fire Departments on this 850 acre fire near Bryans Corner. Two residences and eight outbuildings were lost. Control lines have been completed at this time and resources will be checking the fire regularly. The two homes that were lost were abandoned. The fire was south of the Balko school about a mile and extended 3 miles further south. About 100 personnel were involved. No cause was determined. The fire started just south of road Hollow E0300 between roads Hollow N1270 and Hollow N1280. Or, 5 SW of Balko OK (Lat: 36.57253 N; Lon: -100.73215 W).

Dennison Fire began around 1542CST (Lat: 35.030000 N; Lon: -102.630000 W) or about 2 miles east of Simms Texas in Deaf Smith County just east of the intersection of Farm to Market Road 1412 and County Road N north of Farm to Market Road 1412. Cause: Investigated but Undetermined. Organizations that Gave or Received Mutual Aid: Vega Fire Rescue, Adrian Vol Fire and EMS, Hereford Fire Dept.

The Cadillac fire originated along I40 frontage road and South Dowell Rd, in Potter County outside of Amarillo at approximately 1500CST on February 21st, 2022. Overall, a total of 96 homes, 18 commercial buildings, 98 outbuildings and 37 other camper vehicles were protected from the fire by several organizations, including Texas A&M Forest Service, Randall County Fire Department, Texas Intrastate Fire Mutual Aid System, Potter County Sheriff's Office, Amarillo Fire Department, Amarillo Medical Services, Atmos Energy, American Red Cross, Amarillo Police Department, Amarillo Emergency Service (AES), Texas Department of Transportation and Xcel Energy. Additionally, 4 residential structures and 11 outbuildings were lost.

One home saved. None lost or damaged. No injuries or fatalities. Organizations that Gave or Received Mutual Aid: Perryton Fire Department, Allison Volunteer Fire Dept, Booker VFD, Canadian VFD, Follett Fire Dept., Higgins/ Lipscomb VFD, Hoover Volunteer Fire Dept., Locust Grove Volunteer Fire Department, Miami/Roberts County VFD.

The majority of Cimarron County started March in exceptional (D4) drought with the far southern stretch in extreme (D3) drought. By the end of the first week the southeast slipped into exceptional drought with the rest of the northern county. Conditions remained very dry through the month with Boise City only measuring 0.19 and Kenton only measuring  0.17 over the course of the month. This is still an inch below normal for the month across the county.

Texas County started the month with the western third to half of the county in exceptional (D4) drought while the rest of the county was in extreme (D3) drought. By the end of the first week continuing dry conditions helped the whole county to fall into exceptional drought. Some relief came to the far eastern portions of the county with the southeast ending the month in extreme drought. Overall the month of March finished around one inch below normal for the month.

Beaver County started the month of March in extreme (D3) drought. By the middle of the month the southwest half of the county slipped into exceptional (D4) drought. Some relief came in the form of snow in the second half of the month. This allowed the eastern third of the county to improve to severe (D2) drought and some improvement to the part of the southwest that fell into exceptional drought. Only a small portion of the far northwest corner of the county ended the month in exceptional drought.  The far eastern portion of the county ended the month near normal for precipitation, while the rest of the county ended half to one inch below normal for the month.

Dallam County started the month in extreme (D3) drought. By the end of the first week the northeast quarter of the county fell into exceptional (D4) drought. Although some precipitation was received in portions of the county during the month, the county remained in D3 to D4 through the end of the month as a 4���- 6��� deficit going back 365 days continued.

Sherman County started the month of March in extreme (D3) drought. By the end of the first week the continuing dry conditions led to almost the entire county degrading into exceptional (D4) drought. Many locations across the county only received a 0.1 to 0.2 of moisture during the month leading to a continuation of a 4 to 12 deficit over the past 365 days.

Hansford County started the month in extreme (D3) drought. By the end of the first week the the entire county slipped into exceptional (D4) drought as dry conditions continued. A late month snow storm  brought some relief to the eastern half to two thirds of the county. This was just enough to improve eastern portions of the county back to extreme drought. Western portions remained in a 4 to 12 deficit over the past 365 days while eastern portions of the county remained in a 2 to 6 deficit over the past 365 days.

Ochiltree County started the month in extreme (D3) drought. By mid month the entire county fell into exceptional (D4) drought. A late month storm system helped the county improve back to extreme drought by the 22nd. Northern portions of the county remained in a 4 to 10 deficit over the past 365 days. The rest of the county remained in a 4 to 6 deficit over the past 365 days.

Lipscomb County started the month out in extreme (D3) drought. By mid month all but the northwest corner of the county had degraded into exceptional (D4) drought. A late month snow storm helped the county finish the month with the western third in extreme drought while the eastern two thirds finished the month in severe (D2) drought.  The county remained in a 4 to 8 deficit over the past 365 days.

Hartley County started and finished the month of March classified in extreme (D3) drought. A small amount of moisture fell during the month, but only enough to keep the county from falling into exceptional (D4) drought. The county remained in a 2 to 8 deficit from the end of the month back 365 days as soil conditions remained very dry.

Moore County started the month in extreme (D3) drought conditions. By the end of the first week the northeast two thirds of the county slipped into exceptional (D4) drought. A late month snow storm only improved the far southeast corner of the county back into extreme drought.  The county remained in a 4 to 8 deficit over the past 365 days.

Hutchinson County started the month in extreme (D3) drought conditions. By the end of the first week the entire county fell into exceptional (D4) drought conditions. A late month snow storm brough some needed relief and brought at least one categorical improvement to all but the far northwest corner of the county. The far southeast corner of the county improved two categorical improvements back to severe (D2) drought. The county remained in a 2 to 6 deficit going back 365 days. The drought conditions also contributed to a wildfire that burned 1500 acres on the 29th.

Roberts County started out in extreme (D3) drought. By the end of the first week the western half to two thirds of the county degraded into exceptional (D4) drought. A late month snow storm helped improve conditions a bit with  the northwest half of the county ended the month in extreme drought while the southeast half of the county ended the month in severe (D2) drought. The county remained in a 4 to 6 defecit dating back 365 days. Drought conditions contributed to a wildfire that burned 39,568 acres that started on March 29th and ended on April 2nd. Several structures were lost in this fire.

Hemphill County started the month in extreme (D3) drought conditions. Two weeks in and all but the far southwest degraded into exceptional (D3) drought conditions. Late in the third week a snow storm brought some much needed moisture with all but the northwest corner of the county improving and ending the month in severe (D2) drought conditions. The county remained in the a 4 to 6 deficit going back 365 days. Drought conditions contributed to a wildfire that burned 7500 acres on the 29th.

Oldham County started the month in extreme (D3) drought conditions. During the third week a storm system moved through improving the south to southeast two thirds of county and ending the month in severe (D2) drought. The county ended the month in 4 to 6 deficit dating back 365 days.

Potter County started the month in extreme (D3) drought conditions. By the end of the first week the far eastern third of the county slipped into exceptional (D4) drought. During the third week a storm system brought some much needed rain to the area improving most of the county to severe (D2) drought conditions for the end of the month.  By the end of the month the county remained in a 4 to 6 deficit dating back 365 days. Drought conditions contributed to a wildfire that burned 1167 acres from the 3rd through the 6th.

Carson County started the month in extreme (D3) drought. By the end of the first week the entire county slipped into exceptional (D4) drought due to prolong periods with no precipitation. A storm system that moved through by the beginning of the third week brough some much needed precipitation. Many places received  an inch to 2 plus on the 21st through the 22nd. This improved the county out of exceptional drought status and into severe (D2) drought status to end the month. Despite this event, the county remained in a 4 to 6 deficit dating back 365 days. Drought conditions contributed a a wildfire that burned 363 acres on the 28th.

Gray County started the month in extreme (D3) drought. By the end of the first week the western half to two thirds of the county fell into exceptional drought. A storm system brought much needed precipitation the 21st into the 22nd with many places across the county receiving an inch to 2 of precipitation. This allowed the county to end the month in severe (D2) status. Despite this relief the county remained in a 4 to 6 deficit dating back 365 days. The drought conditions also contributed to a wildfire that burned 984 acres from March 31st to April 1st.

Wheeler County started the month in extreme (D3) drought conditions. Halfway through the month of the northeastern third of the county fell into exceptional (D4) drought status. By the end of the third week the a storm system brought 1 to 2 of precipitation on the 21st to 22nd. This helped the county end the month in severe (D2) drought for all but the far southeast corner of the county that remained in extreme drought. Despite the improvements the county remained in a 4 to 6 deficit dating back 365 days.

Deaf Smith County started the month in extreme (D3) drought conditions. Most of the county remained in extreme drought by the end of the month with many areas only receiving 0.25 to 0.5 of precipitation during the month. The northwestern and northeastern corner of the county received closer to 0.75 to 1 allowing for these isolated areas of the county to improve to severe (D2) drought status by the end of the month.

Randall County started the month with the western and northern portions in extreme (D3) drought conditions with the rest of the central to southeastern areas in severe (D2) drought. After the first week the entire area in severe drought degraded into extreme drought. The far northeastern corner even slipped into exceptional (D4) drought.  A storm system moved through the 21st to the 22nd bringing some much needed moisture. The northeastern half received the most rain, anywhere from 0.5 to 1 of precipitation. All in all the entire county was able to improve one category into severe (D2) drought. Despite the relief the county remained in a 4 to 6 deficit dating back 365 days.

Armstrong County started the month with the northern third to half of the county in extreme (D3) drought conditions while the rest of the southern county was in severe (D2) drought. By the end of the first week the areas of extreme drought slipped into exceptional (D4) drought while the areas of severe drought slipped into extreme drought.  A storm system in moved through during the 21st to 22nd. This system brought 1 to just above 2 for much of the area. This brought the entire county back into severe drought conditions to end the month. Despite the precipitation the county remained in a 4 to 6 deficit dating back 365 days.

Collingsworth County started the month in extreme (D3) drought conditions. By the end of the first week conditions in the far southeast worsened and fell into exceptional (D4) drought. The storm system that moved through the 21st to 22nd only really brought significant amounts of water to the northwestern third of the county. This portion was able to improve to severe (D2) drought while the southeast stayed in the respective extreme to exceptional drought categories. The county ended the month with a 4 to 12 deficit dating back 365 days.

Donley County started the month in extreme (D3) drought with the exception of the far southwest corner that was in severe (D2) drought to start the month. By the end of the first week the northwest corner of the county was in exceptional (D4) drought while the rest of the county was in extreme drought.  A storm system moved through the area during the 21st to the 22nd where much of the county received 1 to 2. The exception was the far southeast corner that received less than an inch which remained in extreme drought at the end of the month. The rest of the county improved to severe (D2) drought.

The Dalmatian Fire started at approximately 3 pm on March 3,2022 and burned approximately 1,167 acres before it ended on March 6th. Texas A&M Forest Service (TAMFS) had responded to a human caused wildfire in Potter County. Resources on scene are TAMFS Amarillo Task Force, Potter County Fire Department, and National Parks Service. An evacuation was ordered for the Fain Gas Plant. No reported structures lost or damaged.

The 6666 Complex Fire was caused by downed power lines and burned 363 acres through March 28th. Organizations that gave or received Mutual Aid: Borger Fire Dept, Burnett (6666) Ranch, Crutch Ranch VFD, Fritch VFD, Hoover Volunteer Fire Dept., local county resources, National Park Service, Skellytown Volunteer Fire Dept, and the White Deer Volunteer Fire Department.

The Canadian River Bottom Fire started on March 29th and continued through April 2nd. It started between the towns of Canadian and Miami off of highway 60. Canadian Volunteer Fire Department were first resources on scene. Multiple fire department had arrived throughout the evening. Fire crews worked throughout the night establishing containment on both flanks and doing structure protection with heavy equipment and engines. High winds continued throughout the night which kept fire activity very active. In total, 29 structures and 11 vehicles/farm equipment were lost. Livestock relocation was done at the Canadian Rodeo Arena where pens and horse stalls were available for animal relocation. On underground gas pipeline was burning and the company was notified which they shut down the pipeline. The estimated total acreage burned was 39,568 when it ended at the end of shift on April 2nd.

Most of the county was in exceptional (D4) drought going into the month of April, with the exception of an area in the far southwest that was in extreme (D3) drought. Dry conditions continued well into April with most if not all events in the Panhandles missing the far western Oklahoma Panhandle. By the 2nd week all of the county was in exceptional drought. There was still a 8 to 12 deficit dating back 365 days.

The majority of the county was in exceptional (D4) drought at the start of the month. The one exception was the far southeast corner of the county that was in extreme (D3) drought. Dry conditions continued through the month over an inch below normal. The extreme to exceptional drought conditions lasted through the end of the month as the county remained in an 8 to 12 deficit dating back 365 days.

In March the far eastern portion of the county had made some progress on lowering the rainfall deficit and started the month in severe (D2) drought while the rest of the county was in extreme (D3) drought. The was a small section of the northwest in exceptional (D4) drought. Conditions remained dry through the month of April and the far eastern portion slipped back into extreme drought by the end of the third week. The county remained in a 6 to 10 deficit dating back 365 days. These drought conditions did lead to multiple wildfires one of which was a large wildfire that burned 24,542 acres claiming two residence buildings and the injuries of two Balko Fire Fighters. A total of 30,238 acres were able to burn in the county over the course of April due to drought.

The majority of the county started the month of April out in extreme (D3) drought with the far northeastern corner in exceptional (D4) drought. Within the first week conditions worsen and the majority of the county found itself in exceptional drought with the exception of a small section in the southeast stayed in extreme drought for only one more week before the who county was in exceptional drought. The county remained in a 6 to 12 inch deficit dating back 365 days.
Sherman County started and ended the month of April in exceptional (D4) drought. Conditions remained dry with the county remaining in an 8 to 12 inch rainfall deficit dating back 365 days.

The far western portion of the county started the month of April already in exceptional (D4) drought with the rest of the county in extreme (D3) drought. Within the first week the northwest half was in exceptional drought with the southeastern half in extreme drought and stayed this way through the end of the month. The county remained in a 6 to 10 inch deficit for rainfall dating back 365 days.

The county started the month out with the entire county in extreme (D3) drought. There was a very temporary improvement in the southeastern half during the first week to severe (D2) drought. By the middle of the month the entire county was back in extreme drought despite a late rain event with much of the county receiving 0.25 to 0.5 inches of rain. The county remained in a 6 to 10 inch deficit going back 365 days.

Lipscomb County started the month with the western third in extreme (D3) drought and the rest of the county in the severe (D2) drought. Conditions remained dry with very minimal rainfall for the month leading to the entire county ending up in extreme drought by third week of the month. The county remained in a 6 to 10 deficit dating back 365 days.

The entire county started out in extreme (D3) drought. Conditions remained dry with the northern two thirds of the county falling into exceptional (D4) drought by the second week. A late month rain event produced couple inches of rain the far northeastern potion of the county allowing that area to improve and go back into extreme drought.  The majority of the county remained in a 6 to 10 deficit dating back 365 days at the end of the month.

The northeastern portion of the county started the month in exceptional (D4) drought with the rest of the southwest in extreme (D3) drought. The majority of the month remained extremely short on rainfall. However, a late month event on the 28th produced 2 inch plus of rain across the northern half of the county. This one event improved the area of exceptional drought and back into extreme drought.

The majority of Hutchinson County started the month in extreme (D3) drought conditions with the far northwest in exceptional (D4) drought and the far southeast in severe (D2) drought.  Conditions remained mostly dry through the month with the whole county getting close to be classified in exceptional drought. A late month event dropped a couple inches of rain keeping the the county in extreme drought and even improving the northwest corner by one category. The county remained in a 6 to 10 inch deficit dating back 365 days by the end of the month.

Roberts County started the month out with the northwest half in extreme (D3) drought and the southeast half in severe (D2) drought. Despite a late month event where areas received 0.5 inches up to 2 inches the deficit for the last 365 days has did not change much allowing the whole county to end the month in extreme drought. The county ended the month in a 6 to 10 inch deficit dating back 365 days.

The majority of the county started the month in severe (D2) drought. The majority of the month remained dry leading to the entire county falling into extreme (D3) drought by the end of the month. The county remained in a 4 to 8 inch deficit dating back 365 days.

The far northern portion of the county started the month in extreme (D3) drought with the rest of the southern portions in severe (D2) drought. Overall the month was very dry and the entire county ended the month in extreme drought. The county remained in a 6 to 10 inch dating back 365 days.  These drought conditions also contributed to at least one grass fire that burned 746 acres.

Potter County started the month in severe (D2) drought. With little to no spring rains for relief the county quickly fell into extreme (D3) drought. This was not good for many spring time high wind events falling fueling wildfires. Multiple wildfires broke out in the county during the month of April as fuels remained extremely dry.  The county ended the month in a 6 to 10 inch deficit dating back 365 days. These drought conditions helped to contribute to two wildfires over the course of the month. One of which was a large fire that burned 25,609 acres with no property damage. One other fire was only 553 acres but started near homes which lead to 5 homes being lost with high winds also feeding spread.

Carson County started the month in severe (D2) drought. Conditions remained dry with well below normal precipitation for the month. This led to the county falling into extreme (D3) drought and ending the month this way. The county remained in a 6 to 10 inch deficit dating back 365 days.

Gray County started the month in severe (D2) drought. Conditions remained dry with well below normal precipitation for the month. This led to the county falling into extreme (D3) drought and ending the month this way. The county remained in a 6 to 10 inch deficit dating back 365 days.

Wheeler County started the month in severe (D2) drought. Conditions remained dry with well below normal precipitation for the month. This led to the county falling into extreme (D3) drought and ending the month this way. The county remained in a 6 to 10 inch deficit dating back 365 days. These drought conditions contributed to two grass fires over the course of the month leading to a total of 9,652 acres being burned. No known structures or property was lost in these fires.

The majority of the county was in extreme (D3) drought at the start of the month with the exception of the northeast and northwest corners that were in severe (D2) drought. The month of April was extremely dry with little to no rain. Within the first week the areas of severe drought fell into extreme drought with the rest of the county where it stayed through the end of the month. The county remained in a 6 to 10 inch deficit dating back 365 days. These drought conditions also contributed to at least 2 grass fires that burned a total of 1,119 acres.

Randall County started the month in severe (D2) drought. With in the first week the far southwest corner fell into extreme (D3) drought. By the 2nd week the rest of the county fell into extreme drought where it stayed through the end of the month. Little to no rain fell during the month leaving the county in a 6 to 10 inch rainfall deficit dating back 365 days. These drought conditions also contributed to two known grass fires that burned a total of 721 acres.
Armstrong County started the month in severe (D2) drought. By the second week of the month the entire county fell into extreme drought and remained with a 6 to 10 inch deficit dating back 365 days.

Collingsworth County started the month with the southwest corner in exceptional (D4) drought, extreme (D3) drought through the central part of the county and severe (D2) drought in the northwest corner. The month remained dry with little to no rain leading to the area of severe drought in the northwest falling into extreme drought. The county ended the month with the northwest half to two thirds in extreme drought and the southeast in staying in exceptional drought. The county remained in an 8 to 12 inch rainfall deficit dating back 365 days.

Donley County started the month in severe (D2) drought within the first couple of weeks the entire county fell into extreme (D3) drought and stayed there through the month. The county remained in a 6 to 10 inch rainfall deficit dating back 365 days.

Most of Beaver County started the month of May in extreme (D3) drought, with the exception of a couple of small portions of the far western areas of the county in exceptional (D4) drought. A couple of rain events that dropped  between 1.5 and almost 3 of rain, mainly in the cetral to southeastern half of the county allowed much of the southeast to improve to severe (D2) drought and even moderate (D1) drought status. Even though much of the southeastern portion of the county ended the month near normal the rainfall deficit going back 365 days remains around 6 to 12 below normal.

The majority of Texas County started the month of May in exceptional (D4) drought with a small portion to the southeast in extreme (D3) drought. Within the first couple of days the far southeast slipped into exceptional drought as well, while a a sliver of the north-central portion of the county improved to extreme drought. By the end of the month conditions only improved slightly with the county ending around an inch below normal for the month. There was a sliver of the far northern portion of the county that remained in exceptional drought while the rest of the county to the south had improved to extreme drought. The majority of the county remained with a 6 to 12 defecit dating back 365 days at the end of the month.

The entirety of Cimarron County started the month of May in exceptional (D4) drought. The month of May only brought between 1.5 and 2 of rain. However, this was not enough to any major dent in the deficit that had been racked up well into the late summer of last year.  Much of the county still ended the month with an 8 to 12 deficit going back 365 days. As well as a 2 to 4 deficit dating back 60 days with the exception of the the far southern to southeast portion of the county which managed to see a one category improvement and ended up in extreme (D3) drought.

Dallam County started the month of May entirely in exceptional (D4) drought. A few rain events through out the month allowed most of the county to improve to the extreme (D3) drought status. The far western portion of the county remained in D4 at the end of the month. The county remained in a 4 to 12 defecit dating back 365 days, at the end of the month. Two different wildfires broke out during the month. One of which started in Deaf Smith County which burned a combined 3717 acres with 3 structures lost.

Sherman County started the month of May of in exceptional (D4) drought. Some releif came in May with some late month rain events. However, the month still fell short of normal and conditions only improved to extreme (D3) drought. The county still remained in a 4 to 10 deficit dating back 365 days, at the end of the month.

Hansford County started the month of May with the northwest two thirds in exceptional (D4) drought. The southeastern third was in extreme (D3) drought. The county managed to receive some rainfall during the  the month.   However, it was only enough to improve one category. The area of D4 improved to D3 and the area of D3 to the southeast improved to severe (D2) drought. The county remained in a 4 to 10 defecit dating back 365 days, at the end of the month.

Ochiltree County started the month of May already in extreme (D3) drought. A small portion of the far northwest corner of the county slipped into exceptional (D4) drought within the first week. The county received just enought rain after that to improve one category. The small area of D4 to the northwest improved to D3 while the rest of the county improved to severe (D2) drought. The county ended the month with a 4 to 10 defecit dating back 365 days.

Lipscomb County started the month of May in extreme (D3) drought. Some rain fell in the first two weeks with an improvement into severe (D2) drought by mid month. Some additional rain fell in the last half of the month with the majority of the county improving to moderate (D1) drought. The exception being the far northwest corner of the county remained in D2.  The county ended the month with a 2 to 10 deficit dating back 365 days.

Hartley County started the month of May with the northern half to two thirds in exceptional (D4) drought with the remaining southern portion in extreme (D3) drought. During the first half of the month some rain was received in the east where conditions improved to D3 for the northeast. However, the southwest that was in D3 degraded into D4.  Some additiional rain rain was received in the latter half of the month with some areas of D4 improving to D3. However, the majority of the county still remained in D3 at the end of the month with small areas in the far western to southern portion of the county still in D4. The county ended the month with a 6 to 12 defecit dating back 365 days.

Moore County started the month with the northern two thirds of the county in exceptional (D4) drought and the remaining southern portion in extreme (D3) drought. May first brought about some rain upwards of a quarter of inch of rain improving the area of D4 to D3 within the first week. Very minimal rain fell during the month with the county remaining in D3 by the end of the month with the exception of a very small area improving to severe (D2) drought. The county ended the month with a 2 to 8 deficit dating back 365 days. Also, at least one wildfire started during the month which took a total of 6 structures.

Hutchinson County started the month of May in extreme (D3) drought, with the exception of a small portion of the far northtwest corner that was in exceptional (D4) drought. An early rain event in the first couple of days of the month helped the northwest corner to improve to D3 within the first week.  The county received some decent rainfall spread out through the month allowing the majority of the county to improved to severe (D2) drought by months end. The county remained in a 4 to 8 deficit dating back 365 days.

Roberts County started the month out in extreme (D3) drought. A couple of rain events during the beginning of the month improved portions of the eastern part of the county to severe (D2) drought. Some additional rain fell during week three improving the whole county to severe drought with a small portion of the far eastern part of the county improving to moderate (D1) drought.

Hemphill County started the month of May in extreme (D3) drought. By mid month a few good rain events improved all but the far northwest corner of the county to severe (D2) drought. By the end of week three the northwest corner improved to severe drought while the rest of the county improved one more category to moderate (D1) drought where it stood at the end of the month with upwards of 5 of rain being received for the whole month.

Oldham County started the month in extreme (D3) drought. Dry conditions continued through the first half of the month with the majority of the county slipping into exceptional (D4) drought especially when May usually sees an increase in precipitation after the winter months. The exceptional drought lasted through the end of the month with rain totals for the month only being around 0.5 with a normal thats near 3.

Potter County started the month of May in extreme (D3) drought. May was abnormally dry and the vast majority of the county remained in D3 through the end of the month. The exception of the far southeast that managed to received enough rain to improve to severe (D2) drought. The county remained in a 4 to 10 deficit dating back 365 days.

Carson County started the month in extreme (D3) drought. May was below normal on precipitation, but still received enough rainfall (1.5-2.5) in order to be able to improve one category to severe (D2) drought by the end of the month.

Gray County started the month of May in extreme (D3) drought. Over the course of the month a good portion of the county receieved between 2 and 4 allowing at least one category improvement to severe (D2) drought in the northwest and two category improvement to abnormally (D1) Dry to the southeast.

Wheeler County started the month of May in extreme (D3) drought. Over the course of the month a good portion of the county receieved between 2 and 4 allowing at least one category improvement to severe (D2) drought in the southeast and two category improvement to abnormally (D1) Dry to the northwest.

Deaf Smith County started the month of May in extreme (D3) drought. May was abnormally dry for the county with less than an inch of rain received during the month. This lead to the vast majority of the county degrading into exceptional (D4) drought. At least one wildfire started in Deaf Smith County and continued into Oldham county during the month. This fire burned a combined total of 3717 acres between the two counties with 3 structures lost.

Randall County started the month of May in extreme (D3) drought. May rain was well below normal. There was some rain received but only enough for the southeast two thirds to improve to severe (D2) drought. The county remained in a 4 to 10 deficit dating back 365 days.

Armstrong County started the month of May in extreme (D3) drought. Despite receiving below normal rainfall through the month there was enough rain spread out through the month that conditions improved to severe (D2) drought. The county remained in a 4 to 8 deficiti dating back 365 days.

Collingsworth County started the month out in extreme (D3) drought. The southeastern half of the county did not fair well and remained in extreme drought at the end of the month. The northwest, however, received enough rain to end the month in severe (D2) drought.
Donley County started the month of May in in extreme (D3) drought. Rainfall was below normal the month, with just enough rain in order to improve one category to severe (D2) drought.
The Helium Fire was a wildland/grass fire that had an undetermined cause to fire start. There were 40 homes saved, and an additional 20 other structures saved. There were 6 structures lost.
The Scarbar 2 Fire was traced to a lightning start. This fire burned approximately 500 acres.

The 147 Fire started from power lines at CR 29 in Deaf Smith and quickly hit Bridwell Ranch in Oldham and headed towards I-40. There was one home saved, but 3 other structures were lost. Approximately 3717 acres were burned.
The Midpoint Fire (which started as the 147 fire) started in Deaf Smith county but quickly advanced into Oldham County before it was eventually contained. The fire burned approximately 3717 acres.

The tornado traveled across mostly open country damaging mainly|trees along the path. Toward the end of the track, the tornado|did encounter a large sheet metal and wood pole barn and caused|the walls to collapse on the west side of the structure. This led|to a high end EF0 rating for this tornado.

The tornado touched down just southside Dodson and moved across|the south side of town before moving across open fields to the|Oklahoma border. The tornado was relatively wide and exhibited|some signs of being multi vortex on storm chaser video, but|estimated wind speeds were only high end EF0. Along the path,|there were numerous  large tree limbs snapped and a few uprooted|trees. There was damage to roofs and porches of several homes and|some weak out buildings were destroyed. One unanchored travel|trailer was rolled 40 feet and destroyed as well. There were a|few isolated power poles broken, but most remained standing along|the tornado path. The tornado did cross the county line and continued into Harmon County Oklahoma for a short distance.

Cimarron County started the month of June with two thirds of the northwestern portion in exceptional (D4) drought. The other third was in extreme (D3) drought. Monthly rain fall was minimal with only a small portion of the D4 improving to D3 and a very small area in the southeast corner improving to severe (D2) drought.  Much of the county remained near 2 below normal for the month adding to the overall deficit.

Texas County started the month of June with a portion of the north to northwest in exceptional (D4) drought and the rest of the county was in extreme (D3) drought. With much of the county receiving upwards of 1.5 above the monthly normal, the vast majority improved to severe (D2) drought with a small portion of the northwest corner remaining in extreme drought.

The northwest half to two thirds of the county started the month off in extreme (D3) drought  with a tiny portion of the far northwest corner in exceptional (D4) drought.  To the southeast lied severe (D2) drought with moderate (D1) drought for the far southeast corner. Like Texas County much of the area received upwards of 1.5 above the monthly normal allowing for conditions to improve. The areas of D1 and D2 stayed the same with the area of D3 shrinking to the north a bit. Areas in the far east up against Texas County went from D3 to D2.

Dallam County started the month of June with the majority of the the county in extreme (D3) drought. The exception being the far southwest corner that was in exceptional (D4) drought. The biggest change to drought status was a swather that moved from the northwest to the southeast where a slow moving supercell dropped mutliple inches of rain. This swath can be seen in the drought monitor posted June 7th with an improvement to severe (D2) drought. The rest of the county finished the month well below normal for the month with just barely above a half inch of rain, therefore no other changes were made in drought status.

Sherman County started the month of June entirely in extreme (D3) drought. During the month of June the southwest half of the county only received between 0.75 to 1.5 while the northeast received 1.5 to 3.0  of rain. This allowed the northeast to improve to severe (D2) drought while the southwest stayed in extreme drought at the end of the month.

The northwest half of county started the month in extreme (D3) drought conditions while the southeast half was in severe (D2) drought. Most of the county received 1.5 to 2.0 of rain during the month. Although this was below normal for the month it was enough improve conditions by one category. The northwest improved to severe drought while the southeast improved to moderate (D1) drought by the end of the month.

The vast majority of Ochiltree County started the month in severe (D2) drought. The exception was the far northwest corner was in extreme (D3) drought while the far southeast corner was in moderate (D1) drought. With a monthly rain ranging from 1.5 to 3.0 much of the area of severe drought improved to moderate drought especially in the central to southern portions of the county.

Lipscomb County started the month with the northwest corner in severe (D2) drought and the rest of the county in moderate (D1) drought. Limpscomb County only received 0.5 to 1.5 of rain during the month which is well below normal. The monthly rain was just enough to keep degradation from occurring.

Hartley County started the month of June with the majority of the county in extreme (D3) drought with the exception of the far southern and far western portions that  were in exceptional (D4) drought. With the exception of the far eastern portions of the county that received 2 plus there was no change to drought conditions/classification. This area that received 2 plus was able to improve to severe (D2) drought by the end of the month. Also the small area along the far south improved from D4 to D3.  Much of the area that remained in D3 or D4 remained in a 90 day deficit of 2 to 4.

The vast majority of Moore County started the month with extreme (D3) drought conditions. Much of the central to southern portions of the county received 2 to 4 during the month allowing for conditions to improve to severe (D2) drought and even some areas improving to moderate (D1) drought.

The majority of Hutchinson County started the month in severe (D2) drought with a small portion in far southwest in extreme (D3) drought. Much of the county received 2 to 4 over the course of the month allowing most of the county to improve to moderate (D1) drought and abnormally dry (D0) conditions.

The far eastern portion of Roberts County started the month of June in moderate (D1) drought while the majority of the county started the month in sever (D2) drought. Central to eastern portions of the county received 2 to 5 over the course of the month allowing  the far southern and eastern county improve to abnormally dry (D0) and the rest of the county to improve to moderate (D1) drought.

Hemphill County started the month of June in moderate (D1) drought with a small section in the far eastern portion in severe (D2) drought. Much of the county received 3 to 6 of rain during the month allowing the majority of the county to improve to abnormally dry (D0) conditions.

Oldham County started the month of June in exceptional (D4) drought conditions. June was abnormally dry with the majority of the county only receiving 1 to 2 of rain. This only allowed minor improvements and the county ending the month in extreme (D3) drought conditions still.  The 90 day deficit was still around 2 to 6 below normal.

Potter County started the month of June in extreme (D3) drought with the exception of the far southeast corner that was in severe (D2) drought. The county received 1 to 3 of rain during the month with  conditions in the east improving to severe (D2) and moderate (D1) drought conditions, while the west remained in extreme drought.

The majority of Carson County started the month of June in Severe (D2) drought while the far northwest corner of the county was in extreme (D3) drought. Western portions received 2 to 3 while areas in the east to northeast received 3 to 4.5 inches.  This allowed the county to improve one to two categories with the west ending the month in moderate (D1) drought while the east ended the month abnormally dry (D0).

The northwest corner of Gray County started the month of June in severe (D2) drought while the rest of the county to the southeast was in moderate (D1) drought. Much of the county received 3 to 6 allowing for conditions to improve.  This allowed the entire county to finish the month out in abnormally dry (D0).

The southeast corner of Wheeler County started the month of June in severe (D2) drought while the rest of the county to the northwest was in moderate (D1) drought. Much of the county received 4 to 6 allowing for conditions to improve. This allowed the entire county to finish the month out in abnormally dry (D0).

Most the county started the month in exceptional (D4) drought, with a section of the southeast corner that was in extreme (D3) drought. Across the south only an inch or less of rain was received during the month leading to no change in the area of D4 to the south. The north-central portion of the county received 2 plus leading to an improvement to extreme (D3) drought.

The northwest third of the county started the month in extreme (D3) drought while the rest of the county was in severe (D2) drought at the beginning of the month. Most of the county received 2 or less with some areas only receiving half an inch. Basically no changes were made to drought status for Randall during the month of June.

Armstrong County started the month of June in severe (D2) drought.  The northeast corner received 2 to 4 allowing for an improvement to moderate (D1) drought while the rest of the county only received 2 or less leaving conditions in severe drought.

The southeast corner of Collingsworth County started the month of June in extreme (D3) drought conditions, while the northwest half was in severe (D2) drought. The majority of the county received 2 to 6 of rain over the course of the month allowing the  majority of the county to improve to at least moderate (D1) drought with the exception of a portion in the far south that remained in severe drought.

Donley County started the month in severe (D2) drought. The county received 2 to 5.5 through the month allowing the county to improve to moderate (D1) drought with the exception of a small portion in the far southwest corner of the county that remained in severe drought.
