Cimarron County started the month of May with Exceptional Drought (D4) conditions to the east and Extreme Drought (D3) conditions to the west. Unlike areas in the TX Panhandle, Cimarron County only received 2 to 6 of rainfall. This was enough to only wipe out the D3 and D4. However, much of the county ended the month in Severe Drought (D2) and some isolated areas in Moderate Drought (D1).

Texas County started the month of May in really bad shape with widespread Exceptional Drought (D4). The county received 4 to 8 of rainfall through the month, primarily in the latter half. This was enough to reduce  the drought to Extreme Drought (D3) to Severe Drought (D2). This May was the wettest month, with the monthly rainfall equivalent of 50% or more of all of last years annual rainfall.

Beaver County started the month of May with a portion of the southeast in Extreme Drought (D3) while the rest of the county was in Exceptional Drought (D4). The county saw some minor improvements in the southwest with 6 to 10 of rain being received. However, much of the county ended the month either in Extreme Drought (D3) or Severe Drought (D2) conditions.

The western third of Dallam County started the month of May in Exceptional Drought (D4). There was also a small portion of the far east that was in D4 as well. The rest of the county started the month in Extreme Drought (D3).  Western portions of the county received a monthly rainfall of 2 to 5, while the much of the central to eastern portions of the county received 5 to 8 of rainfall. The county ended the month with the western third of the county in Severe Drought (D2), as well as a small portion in the far north. The rest of the county where 5 to 8 were received improved to Moderate Drought (D1).

Hartley County started the month of May with the northwest corner in Exceptional Drought (D4), while the rest of the majority of the county was in Extreme Drought (D3). Much improvement came to central and eastern portions of the county as 6 to 10 of rain was received during the month. Central portions were able to improve to Moderate Drought (D1) while the eastern portion improved to Abnormally Dry (D0). The western portion of the county received 3 to 6 and saw some improvements as well. The western third of the county still ended the month in Severe Drought.

Sherman County started the month of May in Exceptional Drought (D4) with the far southwest corner in Extreme Drought (D3). The county received 6 to 12 of rain over the course of the month, mainly in the last two weeks. The higher end of this rain was across the central to southern portions of the county that ended the month in Moderate Drought (D1) to Abnormally Dry (D0). The lower end of the rain was across the northeastern third of the county where the month ended with Severe Drought (D2).

Moore County started the month of May with the far northeastern corner in Exceptional Drought (D4) and the rest of the county in Extreme Drought (D3).  Much of the county received 8 to 12 of rainfall over the course of the month, primarily in the latter half. All the rain led to conditions gradually improving to Abnormally Dry (D0) by months end.

Hansford County started the month of May in Exceptional Drought (D4). The southern half of the county received a monthly rainfall around 10. Which helped to improve the south to Abnormally Dry (D0) to Moderate Drought (D1). The northern half of the county had only received 4 to 6 of rainfall which did improve conditions ending the month in Severe Drought (D2) across the north.

Two thirds of the northwestern portion of Ochiltree County started the month of May in Exceptional Drought (D4). The rest of the south and east was in Extreme Drought (D3). Much of the county saw 8 to 10 of rain that reduced the drought down to Moderate Drought (D1) by the end of the month.

Lipscomb County started the month in Extreme Drought (D3). Over the course of the month, primarily the latter half, the western half of the county received 5 to 8 of rainfall. This allowed a small area in the east to improve to Moderate Drought (D1). Other areas only received 3 to 5 of rainfall with the rest of the county ending the month in Severe Drought (D2).

Hutchinson County started the month of May with around a third of the northern portion of the county in Exceptional Drought (D4). The rest of the county was in Extreme Drought (D3). Over the course of the month the county received 8 to 12 of rain, mainly in the latter half of the month. This led to the county ending the month in Moderate Drought (D1) to Abnormally Dry (D0).

Roberts County went into the month of May with Extreme Drought (D3) conditions. The county received 6 to 12 of rainfall during the month. The county ended the month of May in Moderate Drought (D1) to Abnormally Dry (D0) conditions.

Hemphill County started the month of May with Extreme Drought (D3). Western and southern portions of the county that received 5 to 6 of rain improved to Severe Drought (D2) by months end while central to northeastern portions of the county that received 3 to 5 stayed in Extreme Drought (D3) at the end of the month.

Oldham County started the month entirely in Extreme Drought (D3). Central to eastern portions of the county received 5 to 10 of rainfall for over the course of the month and improved to Abnormally Dry (D0) and Moderate Drought (D1). The western quarter of the county only received 3 to 5 leaving the county in Severe Drought (D2) at the end of the month.

Deaf Smith County started the month of May with the majority of the county in Extreme Drought (D3), with the exception of a small area in the far eastern portion in Severe Drought (D2). During the month May 5 to just over 10 of rain fell across the county. Hereford alone got almost 10 of rain and experienced some historic flooding issues on 26th and 27th of May. Because of the large amounts of rain received during the month the county was able to end the month in Moderate Drought (D1).

Potter County started the month of May in Extreme Drought (D3). Potter County received between 6 and 10 of rainfall for the month. Improvements were gradual, but the entire county ended the month in Abnormally Dry (D0).

Randall County started the month with northern and western portions of the county in Extreme Drought (D3) with the rest of the county in Severe Drought (D2). Over the course of the month, mainly the latter half, the county saw widespread 5 to 10 of rainfall. This led to overall drought improvement with the county ending the month of May in Moderate Drought (D1) to Abnormally Dry (D0).

Carson County started the month of May with an area of the far northern and far western portion of the county in Extreme Drought (D3). The rest of the county had started the month with Severe Drought (D2) conditions. Rain events were few in number and spread out during the first half of the month. Carson County received enough rain to improve all of the county to Moderate Drought (D1) by May 23rd. With the rain events picking up in frequency the last two weeks of May conditions continued to improve to Abnormally Dry (D0) by the end of the month. The county received   total of 4 to 8 of rain for the month bring much relief, and ultimately ended the drought across the county.

Gray County started the month of May with a small area of the far northwest portion of the county in Extreme Drought (D3), while the rest of the county started in Severe Drought (D2).Rain events were few in number and spread out during the first half of the month. Much needed rain had helped conditions to improve to Moderate Drought (D1) by May 21st.  Western portions of the county received 4 to 8 by the end of the month while eastern portions received 2 to 4 over the course of the month.

Armstrong County started the month of May in Severe Drought (D2). Multiple rain events during the month helped the county improve to Moderate Drought (D1) by May 23rd. With additional rainfall during the last week, much of the county improved to the status of Abnormally Dry (D0).  By months end the county had received 5 to 8 of rain for the month of May.

Wheeler County started the month of May with entire county in Severe Drought (D2). May did come with some good rain events leading to the majority of the county improving to Moderate Drought (D1) while a small portion of the county remained in D2 at months end. The monthly rainfall for the month ranged from around 1 all the way up to 4 to 5 across Wheeler County.

Donley County started the month of May in Severe Drought (D2) conditions. With numerous rain events throughout the month improvements were made in the drought. The majority of the county had improved to Moderate Drought (D1) with the exception of around a quarter of the county in the southeast corner that stayed in D2 during the last week of the month. However, additional rainfall on May 31st helped to wipe out the rest of the D2 in the southeast. Eastern portions of the county had received 1 to 3 of rain over the course of the month, while areas in the west had received 3 to 5 by months end.

The northwestern half of Collingsworth County started the month of May in Severe Drought (D2), while the southeastern half was in Extreme Drought (D3). May rain started off slow, but eventually picked up and improved much of the county. By May 23rd the majority of the county improved to Moderate Drought (D1). D2 conditions stayed in the far southwest corner and much of the far eastern portion of the county. Monthly rainfall totals ranged from 0.5 to around 6.

The vast majority of Cimarron County started the month of June with Severe Drought (D2) conditions, with some small areas with Moderate Drought (D1). A wet pattern continued to take place across much of the area going into June. This helped conditions improve with a one category improvement across the county by mid month ending all of D2 in the area. Much of the county saw 5 to 8 of rainfall over the month with county ending the month with only Abnormally Dry (D0) in the area.

The majority of Texas County started the month of June in Severe Drought (D2) conditions with small areas of Moderate Drought (D1) in the northwest and southeast corners. A wet pattern continued across much of the area going into June with D2 improving to D1 by mid month. The county received a monthly rainfall of 3 to 8 allowing much of the county to end June with Abnormally Dry (D0) conditions.

Beaver County started the month of June with an area in the north and northeast in Extreme Drought (D3). The southwest corner was in Moderate Drought (D1) with the rest of the county in Severe Drought (D2) . The area of D3 had improved to D2 by mid month, and much of the area that was in D2 improving to D1. By the third week the rest of the D2 had improved to D1, leaving the north in Moderate Drought (D1) and the south was Abnormally Dry (D0). Five to ten inches of rain fell across the county during the course of the month.

Sherman County started the month of June with Severe Drought (D2) conditions across the northeastern third of the county. A wet pattern continued through the early part of the month allowing for the area of D2 to improve to Moderate Drought (D1) by mid month. Rain events continued with the area of D1 improving to Abnormally Dry (D0) conditions by the third week. The county received a total of 3 to 6 over the course of the month.

The northwestern third to half of the county was in Severe Drought (D2) at the beginning of the month. Several rain events during the beginning of the month continued improving conditions with the area of D2 improving to Moderate Drought (D1) with the rest of the county by mid month. The county received a monthly total of 2 to 6 ending the month with Abnormally Dry (D0) conditions across the north and normal conditions across the south.

The far western quarter or so of Oldham County started the month of June with Severe Drought (D2) conditions. The rest of the county to the east was in Moderate Drought (D1) to Abnormally Dry (D0). By the second week there was a one category improvement across the county.  The western portion that was in the worse condition received upwards of 5 of rain over the course of the month while the rest of the county received 2 to 5. This left he county in D0 to the west and no category on the drought monitor in the east at the end of the month.

A small area of Severe Drought (D2) existed in the northeast corner of Wheeler County at the beginning of the month. Several back to back rain events occurred in the beginning of the month lead to much of the county to rid itself of drought by mid month.  The county had received 8 to 12 of rain for the entire month.

The majority of Lipscomb County started the month of June in Severe Drought (D2).  Rain events continued to slowly improve conditions through the month with D2 finally improving to Moderate Drought (D1) by the third week. The county received 3 to 8 of rain over the course of the month ending June in Abnormally Dry (D0) conditions.

Several rain events continued through much of June improving conditions to Moderate Drought (D3) by the third week. The county received around 4 to 8 of rain over the course of the month leaving the county in Abnormally Dry (D0) conditions at months end.

About a third of the western portion of the county started the month of June with Severe Drought (D1) conditions. An area of D2 also existed across the far northern conditions up against the Oklahoma Panhandle. Continued rain events through the month had most of the areas of D2 improving to D1 by mid month. The exception being the far southwest corner of the county that did not improve to D1 until the third week. Much of the county received 5 to 8 of rain over the course of the month allowing for the county to end the month with Abnormally Dry (D0) conditions.

The western third of the county started the month of June in Severe Drought (D2) conditions. Areas to the east were in Moderate Drought (D1) to Abnormally Dry (D0) conditions. The Severe Drought in the west took some time but eventually got wiped out by the third week. An additional 2 to 6 fell over the course of the month with the county ending the month with D0 across the western two thirds.

A small area in the far southeast corner of the county had started and ended the month in Severe Drought (D2). This area in the southeast received less than 2 for the entire month leaving it in drought at months end.

This tornado developed near County Road 17 and produced some minor tree damage, with limbs and branches being blown down. The tornado then continued across open field before impacting a residence just off Highway 277, where it brought down trees and some power lines along that road. As it crossed Highway 277, it brought down about 7 power poles, and caused more impressive tree damage, snapping branches and some trees while uprooting other hardwood trees. It resulted in some minor roof damage to a shed and damaged another shed at a natural gas facility. The tornado then crossed County Road 22, just to the south of Highway 277. Here, it snapped several hardwood branches and uprooted another tree. It also lifted the lids off of two silos, one of which collapsed in on the side. The debris of the lids ended up damaging a nearby barn. The tornado then crossed open fields and Highway 277 once more before causing some minor tree branch damage along Highway 2124. The tornado likely lifted after this point.

The entire county of Deaf Smith County was in Moderate Drought (D1) through the month of September. Going into the beginning of October the western fourth to third of the county slipped into Severe Drought (D3) and stayed in D3 through the end of the month. Potter County continued to see dry conditions with an area of Severe Drought (D2) in the central to southwestern portions of the county, and Moderate Drought (D1) elsewhere sticking around for the entire month. This was due to a long dry streak starting around the end of June.

This fire, the L Road fire, was human caused and was located 9 miles north of Guymon near Highway 136 and L Road. It burned 323 acres and cost an estimated $200,256. A couple of abandoned structures and a barn was lost.

The cause of this fire was unknown. Fire was located just northeast of Slapout, OK and burned 26,020 acres and continued to remain active through March 8th. Estimated costs of the fire from the Forestry Service were around $323,000. Damage estimations from the fire from the OSU Extension Service included the loss of 504 head of cattle, 35,000 bales of hay, 3 occupied houses and 1 unoccupied house, 12 barns and 1 solar array. This is approximately 2.3% of pastureland in the county that was temporarily removed from production, and 7.4% of the county cow inventory that either perished in the fire or was subsequently culled or euthanized due to injury. Estimated losses based on this information sum to a total of $8.73 million in damages, or $335 per burned acre.||Estimated cattle industry losses in Beaver County include $1.62 million in fencing costs. This includes damaged fence removal ($49 thousand) and replacement ($1.4 million) for 70% of burned pastures and fence repair ($179,000) for the remaining 30% of burned pastures. Emergency feeding ($87,000), cattle injury assessment and treatment ($24,000), and temporarily holding cattle on emergency grazing such as CRP land while pastures recuperate ($858,000) bring the cost of treating and maintaining displaced cattle to $969,000. The value of cattle who perished in the fire or had to be euthanized due to injury was estimated as $1 million, with an additional $1 million in market value loss for cows that were culled due to fire injury. Carcass disposal was estimated at $63,000. In addition, the hay that was lost in the fire was valued at $2.35 million. A total of $1.7 million in structures lost was estimated.

With only 0.12 to 0.14 of rain measured across Beaver County in March and 0.44 to 0.65 in April the county quickly degraded to Moderate Drought (D1). By the first of May conditions worsened as precipitation kept lacking the northeastern half fell into Severe Drought (D2). By the end of the month over 90 percent of the county was in D2.

For several months Lipscomb County had below normal precipitation. By the first of the month the county fell into Moderate Drought (D1) with the northeastern corner of the county in Severe Drought (D2). With May rains being below normal the county stayed in these drought categories through the whole month.

This tornado touched down after the initial parent tornado occluded. Based on spotter/chaser video, it appears to have developed in about the same locations as the first Clarendon tornado. It became wide, likely going over the same locations as the previous tornado. It then started to follow the rim of the mesocyclone, likely being more of a satellite tornado around the main mesocyclone. The tornado was recorded as being on the ground for about 15 minutes before finally lifting. It likely did not move very fast before finally becoming corkscrew in nature before lifting. Damage seems to be limited to mesquite brush damage. However, the worst known damage was to a water pumping windmill which was toppled and destroyed by the tornado. The maximum estimated winds were 90mph.

A small portion of the northeastern corner of Lipscomb County entered the month of June in Severe Drought (D2) with  a small area in the southwest corner in Abnormally Dry (D0) status, and Moderate Drought (D1) across the majority of the county in between. The are of D2 in the northeast improved to D1 during the first week of the month. However, much of the county remained in D1 to D0 status by months end.

At the beginning of the month roughly 80 to 90 percent of Beaver County was in Severe Drought (D2). A wet pattern starting in the end of May and beginning of June shrank the area of D2 to the west central part of the county, just outside of the town of Beaver within the first week of June. A break in the rains occurred with another wet pattern about mid month and the rest of D2 being wiped out along with much of the county leaving the Moderate Drought (D1) category as well. An Oklahoma mesonet located near Beaver measured a grand total of 9.27 for the month of June. This allowed for all drought categories around Beaver and western parts of the county to be completely wiped out. The mesonet near Slapout received 6.18 and a small area of D1 stayed in the southeast corner of the county.

This a continuation of the Feb 27th Wildfire that started at 14:28 CST.  Cause unknown. Fire was located just northeast of Slapout, OK and burned 26,020 acres and continued to remain active through March 8th.  Estimated costs of the fire  $323,000.

The 687 Reamer fire started 7.6 miles south of Stinnett and grew to 2000 acres. The fire was initially reported at 1:23pm but not reported to Texas Forest Service until after 10:30pm.  It was within close proximity to the Smokehouse creek fire and did eventually merge into that fire. This fire was caused when a broken power pole led to utility wires coming into contact with fuels on the ground. There is no estimated cost of this fire. but there was a one fatality.  An 83 year old woman was trapped in her home that became engulfed in flames around the town of Stinnett.  The fire was noted 100 percent contained on a March 1st sit rep report.

At approximately 3:10 pm on February 26, 2024, Texas A&M Forest service received a request for assistance for a wildfire in Gray County.  This fire was named the Grape Vine Creek Fire.  The fire started 9.5 miles southwest of Lefors, Texas.  The fire burned a total of 34,883 acres and cost an estimated $234,000. It wasn't contained until March 10th around 2:44pm CST. According to a state of Texas report on the wildfires, a three-wire power pole located in Gray County, just to the south of Pampa, broke and crashed to the ground, bringing the wires in contact with fine grassy fuels and ignited the Grape Vine Creek Fire.

The Magenta Fire ignited just before a cold front came through on Feb 27th.  The fire was located just north of the town of Boys Ranch, or seven miles to the south of Channing along US Highway 385.  The fire was held to 3297 acres.  The fire was contained by March 5th. The cause of the fire was undetermined.

The far southeastern corner of Donley County into the southeastern third of Collingsworth County started the month of October in Severe Drought (D2). There was a small area of Extreme Drought (D3) in the far southeastern corner of Collingsworth County.  By mid month, the extended dry conditions allowed the area of D3 to grow, taking over much of the southeastern third to half of Collingsworth County and even the far southeastern corner of Donley County. The area of D2 only spread to the northwest ever so slightly. By month's end just over 50% of Collingsworth County was in D3 with the rest of the northeastern parts of the county in D2. November 2nd brought in quite the prolonged rain event to the combined OK/TX Panhandles, especially the southeastern half where 2 to 3 fell. This was 2 to 3 times the normal monthly rainfall for the area and allowed parts of Donley, Wheeler, and Collingsworth counties that were in Extreme Drought (D3) and Severe Drought (D2) to improve a category  by the end of the first week of November. Two more events occurred within the first half of November, allowing all areas to be removed from all drought fully and completely.  Donley, Wheeler, and Collingsworth counties received a total of 8 to 10 of rain by the middle of the month. This amount of rain in November is not common at all and well received for the removal of drought.

Heavy rainfall resulted in up to eight inches of standing water along 23rd and 25th avenues on the north side of Pampa.
Nickel to quarter size hail fell for a few minutes in Fritch.

A supercell thunderstorm produced a swath of hail across portions northern Hutchinson County to the northeast of Pringle. Initially hail of quarter size fell just outside of Pringle but the hail increased in size as the supercell continued to move to the north and east. Measured hail increased to billiard ball and tennis ball size with the maximum observed hail size being three inches in diameter, or around the size of a large apple. Some of this hail was found by spotters after the storm had passed so there may have been some additional melting that occurred.

This tornado touched down in central Roberts County, roughly seven miles to the southeast of Highway 70, to the south of Farm to Market Road 283. The initial touchdown location and time were estimated based on a combination of radar imagery and storm spotter reports. This tornado grew in size very quickly, with several reports of it taking on a cone and stovepipe shape to it. As the tornado tracked to the southeast, it traversed very rugged terrain which did not provide much in the way of damage indicators or survey access. The highest concentration of visual and known damage was along FM 283 near the intersection with FM 2699. Here, there was minor branch and tree damage, but the more significant damage was a center pivot was completely overturned. It also appeared that some part of it was twisted. Given the angle of the pivot to the direction of motion as well as the presence of winter wheat in the field, it is probable that it took a higher wind speed to flip this pivot and this is one place where the highest rating occurred, somewhere between 105-110mph.  The tornado then continued to the southeast, crossing FM 283 a few times. Along FM 283, near Quarter Horse Road, the tornado downed a power pole and twisted barbed wire fencing. Additional large branches were blown in this area. As the tornado once again crossed FM 283 south of Quarter Horse Road, it downed nine additional power poles. All along its track, surveyors noted several traffic warning signs bent over at the base and even some were broken and twisted at the base, and from the ground. The tornado traveled just to the north of Miami, with no known damage to the town. Storm spotters indicated it crossed Highway 60 before dissipating. Little damage was noted but the ending point was depicted on the south side of the highway per visual confirmation. The maximum estimated wind speed was 110mph.
A heat burst occurred around 2030 CDT from decaying thunderstorms. This resulted in a few large tree branches being snapped to the east northeast of Goodwell.
Hail ranging from golfball size to hen egg size fell along Texas Highway 214.
Hail accumulated in a few inches with the hailstones ranging from nickel to quarter size.

This was a very weak and brief tornado. It dropped down just to the south of McCormick Road, along Burrell Street. It resulted in some minor tree damage and tossed a trampoline in another resident's yard. It took a very narrow path to the northeast and|caused some damage to a barn near McCormick Road. The maximum estimated winds were 74mph.

This tornado started around Northridge Drive where it brought down some tree limbs, It then crossed Hunsley Road where it began to impact homes, resulting in roof damage and fencing damage. It caused some fencing damage and minor roof damage to Freedom Fellowship Church. It then moved through the Madison Park subdivision, turning more to the west and following along Tatum Schulte Lane and Willeford Lane. Here, several homes received roof damage, fencing damage and some tree damage. Many of the homes sustained damage as a result of failure to the garage or porch roofs. One home had damage to cars and the home as a result|of a camper that went airborne, finally resting on between houses three doors down. The tornado then turned back to the southwest, crossing FM 2590 and causing additional tree and roof damage to some homes along Aztec Road. It crossed Hunsley Road again and the tornado lifted in the field behind a home. The maximum estimated winds were 110mph.

This tornado touched down near County Road K and FM 1058. It caused damage to a property near this intersection, including some minor roofing damage and a few snapped trees. As this tornado crossed FM1058, seemingly tracking to the north to northwest, it broke a couple of power poles. It looked to continue along County Road K, where it deposited some debris and partially overturned an irrigation pivot before lifting. Given limited damage indicators, track of the tornado is also estimated using radar data. The maximum estimated winds with this tornado was 100mph. Thank you to the Deaf Smith County Emergency Management for their help in the completion of this tornado survey.
Half dollar to golfball size hail fell across Hardesty.
A supercell thunderstorm produced half dollar sized hail in Hereford.
Three inches of snow accumulated in southern Hutchinson County around Borger.
The southeastern corner of Moore County near Lake Meredith received upwards of 1.5 of snow.

Snow accumulated across Potter County with amounts ranging from two inches to 4.8 inches, which was observed at the NWS Amarillo office. Roads became slick early in the event which resulted in several vehicle accidents.
Heavy rain during the night of April 25th resulted in flooding of most of the access road near McCormick Road and I-27. It remained covered in water into the next morning and was barely passable.

Heavy rain occurred on the night of April 25th. There was strong evidence that Spring Creek flooded Shady Lake Drive to the point where the road was impassable and water still remained over the road the following morning.

This tornado was viewed by local fire department from the intersection of FM 1057 and FM 1058. Per collaboration with radar imagery it appeared to move slowly to the northeast before dissipating. No known damage occurred with this tornado and has been given the rating of EFU.
Strong winds behind a surface dryline affected Cimarron county the afternoon of the 18th. Wind gusts up to 66 mph were recorded at the mesonet site located one mile south of Black Mesa State Park.
Baseball size hail occurred around 12 miles south of Higgins.

The tornado started near County Road 30 on the very eastern edge of Hemphill County and quickly intensified as it crossed onto property where it produced damage to several buildings and a home. The home sustained some roofing damage and the back corner of the house had a partial uplift of the roof deck. Additional storage buildings were damaged including shed doors blown off and roofs and siding damaged. Several trees were uprooted in the yard. A cattle wind break was partially torn from the ground. The tornado then crossed into Ellis County Oklahoma (NWS Norman forecast area), where it snapped a few tree limbs on E690. The tornado then crossed an open field and the last noted damage was along NS1690 where some large branches were snapped. Based on storm spotter footage and survey, it appears the tornado lifted shortly thereafter.  The tornado was rated an EF1 based on the house damage and the tree damage. The entire track length was around 1.6 miles. The maximum estimated winds were 95mph.
Strong thunderstorm outflow lead to severe wind gusts in Texas county including Goodwell.
Strong thunderstorm outflow lead to severe wind gusts in Texas county, including Guymon.
The mesonet station located one mile east of McLean observed a 60mph wind gust from a few showers that moved across the region.
The mesonet station located four miles east of Wheeler measured a 63mph wind gust from some showers that moved across the area.
Multiple wind gusts in excess of 58 mph occurred between 1934CDT and 2114CDT. Peak wind gusts of 67 mph occurred at 1939CDT under decaying thunderstorms.
The AWOS station located one mile north-northwest of Spearman measured a 61mph wind gust from showers and thunderstorms in the area.
The peak downburst wind gust of 60 mph occurred at 1821CDT with 2 additional gusts of 58 mph shortly after.
The first severe wind gust of 59mph occurred at 2010 CDT, with another 58mph wind gust measured at 2012 CDT and the last 59mph wind gust at 2014 CDT.

A supercell thunderstorm moved across the eastern part of Lipscomb County. It produced hail up to the size of golfballs from roughly seven miles southeast of Lipscomb to Higgins. Quarter size hail fell about seven miles to the northeast of Glazier.
Wind gusts over 60mph occurred for two minutes.

Snow accumulations ranged from around one half of an inch in the western part of the county to one to two inches in the east. The snow accumulation may have been higher but the high winds made measuring snow extremely difficult and even made for times of poor visibility on the 8th.
Hail up to quarter size fell along County Road X.
Quarter to golfball size hail fell on the north side of Howardwick.
Winds gusted between 59 and 68 mph between 2054CDT and 2059CDT.

A swath of quarter to half dollar size hail fell to the north of Lake Tanglewood. Hail of at least quarter size fell near Circle C Trail and Claude Highway. Window and gutter damage occurred as well as some vehicle damage, which included a significant amount of small dents in the hood and top of a pickup truck. Hail broke one window in a chicken coop and damaged a vinyl gutter.
A swath of large hail fell from two miles west of Darrouzett to four miles southeast of Darrouzett. Hail ranged from half dollar size to two inches in diameter.
Baseball size hail fell west of Follett. This resulted in broken windshields o some vehicles in the area.

A supercell thunderstorm that moved through the area roughly eight miles south of Follett produced very large hail. Ping pong ball size hail fell along FM1454 between Follett and Higgins. Additionally, several spotters observed and measured hailstones of 3.24 inches to 3.4 inches. It was likely that some of these stones had melted by the time the measurement had occurred and larger hail may have fallen.
Multiple pictures were received of a well developed funnel cloud that made it roughly 75 percent to the ground. This funnel cloud lasted around 30 seconds to one minute.
Hail ranging from one inch to 1.75 inches fell to the northwest and north of Elmwood.
The mesonet station located eight miles west of Slapout measured a wind gust of 87mph. Winds continued to gust to 61mph through 740pm CDT.

Several photos and videos were submitted of a brief circulation that occurred east of FM 294 and south of County Road 13. The circulation lasted around a minute to a minute and a half. No damage was noted as the tornado remained in open fields.

A supercell thunderstorm slowly moved through and south of Claude. It produced a swath of hail ranging from quarter size to grapefruit size. The largest hailstones that measured 3.5 inches and 4.25 inches occurred around ten miles south of Claude.

A thunderstorm moved over and just to the southwest of Stinnett and produced severe hail. Golfball hail fell over Stinnett. The ICECHIP research team measured several hailstones to the southwest of Stinnett, between one and four miles. These ranged from 24 to 33mm, which when converted to inches is 1.0-1.25 inches.
The mesonet station located 15 miles west southwest of Clarendon gusted to 65 mph at 1640CDT and continued to gust above 58 mph until 1646CDT. The peak gust of 83 mph occurred at 1642CDT.
Fast moving flood waters covered County Road J just off HWY 60. Water was at least 6 to 8 inches deep.
ICECHIP research team provided this measurement.
The mesonet site located at three miles north-northeast of Umbarger measured a wind gust of 72mph.
The mesonet station located three miles north-northwest of Palo Duro Canyon measured a wind gust of 60mph.
The ASOS at the Rick Husband International Airport measured a wind gust of 60mph from non-thunderstorm wind that occurred during the early morning hours of August 3rd.
Six to seven inch diameter tree branches were blown down in the area.
The roof of a barn was blown off on East-West 16 Road.
A localized microburst occurred over south Amarillo, which blew the roof off a metal out-building and drove with wooden posts through the roof of a house.
Multiple tree branches were snapped with some that measured one inch in diameter or larger.
Multiple severe wind gusts were measured at the mesonet site located 12 miles southwest of Dalhart. These gusts ranged from 59mph to 63mph starting around 1525 CDT and lasted through 1535 CDT.
Heavy rain occurred in Palo Duro Canyon, which resulted in flash flooding. The flooding closed a portion of the main road going through the canyon.
Standing water occurred in the outer lanes of US 87 in Canyon.
Hail fell that ranged mostly quarter size to ping pong ball size. However, there were some rogue 2 inch to tennis ball sized hailstones mixed in.

A supercell thunderstorm brought a swath of large hail to portions of Randall County. Baseball size hail was measured in Umbarger. Golfball size hail fell around four miles east northeast of Umbarger, where a windshield was broken of a Canyon Fire Department vehicle that was located along Highway 60 between Umbarger and Canyon. Quarter to golfball size hail fell in Canyon. Ping pong ball to golfball size hail with a few two inch size hailstones fell on the west side of Canyon.
Hail fell that was mainly penny size with a few hailstones up to golf ball size.

A supercell thunderstorm brought a swath of large hail to the areas around Goodwell in Texas County. Baseball size hail fell around six miles west of Goodwell. The largest hailstone that was observed was three inches which occurred three miles southwest of Goodwell. Golfball size hail fell five miles south of Goodwell which resulted in hail damage to trailers and broken windows. Golfball size hail also fell in Goodwell.
Quarter size hail fell about four miles north of Guymon. It produced damage to the side of a house due to wind driven nature of the hail. In addition, golfball size hail fell in Guymon.
Both directions of I-40 at Hope Road were  closed due to water over the roadway.  Traffic was being detoured to the frontage  road.
Main Avenue in Gruver was covered in water.
Windshields were broken from large hail up to 4.5 inches that fell.
Hail dented cars as well as some windows were knocked out of a house.
A decaying thunderstorm produced a minor heat burst over Hooker. The temperature  increased and dewpoint decreased in conjunction with the severe wind gust.
A likely downburst produced a peak wind gust of 59 mph.
These wind gusts likely occurred due to a heat burst.
These wind gusts likely occurred due to a heat burst.
A supercell thunderstorm produced large hail across the city of Panhandle. Hail sizes ranged between golfball and 2 inches on the east side of Panhandle.
Hail up to tennis ball size fell along Highway 287 south of Masterson.
A motorist driving north stopped due to large hail that was estimated to be ping pong ball size.

A supercell thunderstorm moved across Amarillo north of I-40. It produced a swath of hail ranging from half dollar size to golfball size. One injury was noted when a female was moving plants outside and was hit in the head with a hailstone that was around golfball size.
A supercell thunderstorm produced hail from quarter to golfball size to the north and northwest of Canyon.
Mostly dime size hail fell but some stones were as large as quarter size. Trees and vegetation were damaged.
A supercell thunderstorm brought a swath of hail to the southwest part of Amarillo. Hailstones ranged from around quarter size up to golfball size.
Heavy rain produced an estimated 6 to 12 inches of fast flowing water on couple of  residential streets in the northwest part of Amarillo.
An estimated three to four feet of fast flowing water occurred in a normally dry creek bed.
Heavy rainfall brought flooding along Williams Street. At least an inch of water entered a couple of homes in the neighborhood.
A trained spotter estimated wind gusts at the leading edge of a line of storms to be around 65mph.
Lipscomb 8W mesonet station measured a 68 mph wind gust from a collapsing thunderstorm.

A supercell thunderstorm tracked through southern Randall County and produced a swath of large hail from up to seven miles northwest of Canyon, and through the city of Canyon. Hail initially was around ping pong ball size but grew larger as the storm went through Canyon, producing hail up two and a half inches in diameter in Canyon. With measured winds around 70-80mph, much of this hail was wind-driven and produced significant damage to roofs, siding and broke many windows. While the total number of windows broken is unknown, it is at least 35.
Water covered the road near 23rd and 4th Street. Road was passable but up to 4 inches  deep on sides of road.

Several visuals from storm spotters indicated that funnel clouds and perhaps brief touchdowns occurred before this tornado from the same supercell as it crossed western Deaf Smith County. However, this tornado did overturn a couple of pivots south of |County Road 27 and east of Highway 214. This appears to have been the only damage noted from this tornado so the exact length of the track is unknown due to the lack of damage indicators. The estimated wind speed from this tornado was 85mph.
A large healthy tree branch snapped.

A severe thunderstorm moved across portions of Moore County during the early morning hours of August 3, 2025. It produced significant, widespread damage to portions of the county from north of Dumas and especially across the town of Sunray. Based on pictures and radar imagery, it has been determined that this damage is attributed to straight line winds. The most significant damage occurred in Sunray. Here, numerous trees were snapped or uprooted. Several power poles were snapped, center pivots were flipped, a few light poles were bent at the base. The press box at the high school sports complex was destroyed. Other structure damage included destroyed|outbuildings and barns as well as roof damage to homes and businesses. Train|cars were laid on their side off a track between Cactus and Sunray. All of the damage was laid in a pattern that is indicative of straight line winds and no convergence of damage was noted.

This tornado was captured on storm chaser video. It quickly became rain wrapped and therefore it is unclear exactly how long it remained on the ground. It appears to have stayed to the north of Highway 64 in an open field.

This tornado was captured via storm spotter video crossing Highway 207. It was not a well defined tornado but there was definitely circulation that crossed the highway. As it|encountered power lines, it resulted in no damage to them though there was some swaying of the lines as it moved through.
This tornado was documented by storm spotter picture. No damage is known to have occurred from this tornado.

This tornado developed south of W 13th Avenue to the southeast of Spearman, producing its first signs of damage once it crossed CR Y just east of CR 27. EF-1 damage occurred in the area including two small pinyon trees being uprooted with others having branches snapped, as well as metal barns having lost several side and|roofing panels. The tornado continued tracking to the south-southeast, pulling roofing and siding off multiple metal barns near CR AA and CR 28. The strongest damage occurred when it crossed CR 28 to the southeast, snapping several wooden power|poles. This is where the tornado achieved peak intensity and earned the EF-2 rating. In the later stages of its life, the tornado flipped single sections of irrigation pivots just north of FM 281, and again as it crossed into far northeast Hutchinson county before eventually lifting. Along the western edge of the track, there were several instances of damage due to strong winds associated with the rear flank downdraft of the supercell. This included snapped wooden power lines and flipped irrigation pivots. The maximum estimated winds were 115mph. The total track length was around 9.5 miles.

This tornado developed south of W 13th Avenue to the southeast of Spearman, producing its first signs of damage once it crossed CR Y just east of CR 27. EF-1 damage occurred in the area including two small pinyon trees being uprooted with others having branches snapped, as well as metal barns having lost several side and|roofing panels. The tornado continued tracking to the south-southeast, pulling roofing and siding off multiple metal barns near CR AA and CR 28. The strongest damage occurred when it crossed CR 28 to the southeast, snapping several wooden power|poles. This is where the tornado achieved peak intensity and earned the EF-2 rating. In the later stages of its life, the tornado flipped single sections of irrigation pivots just north of FM 281, and again as it crossed into far northeast Hutchinson county before eventually lifting. Along the western edge of the track, there were several instances of damage due to strong winds associated with the rear flank downdraft of the supercell. This included snapped wooden power lines and flipped irrigation pivots. The maximum estimated winds of the tornado was 115mph, which occurred in Hansford County. Winds were around 70mph in Hutchinson County. The max width of the tornado was 150 yards also in Hansford County. Total track length was around 9.5 miles.

This tornado pushed a semi-truck off the highway into a ditch approximately six miles north of Boise City on Highway 287. This tornado was later seen by a storm spotter further to the southeast. There is no known damage otherwise with this tornado.
This tornado was spotted and reported by a storm spotter near the Texas and Oklahoma state line. It was noted as a brief tornado. No other information is given about this tornado.

This tornado remained in open grassland causing no damage. The only damage indicator it crossed was a powerline on E0330 Road which was not damaged. It did result in flattened grass along a portion of its track. The total track length was around 6.6 miles.

This tornado remained in open grassland causing no damage. The only damage indicator it crossed was a powerline on E0330 Road which was not damaged. It did result in flattened grass along a portion of its track. The total track length was around 9.4 miles.
Chasers documented a brief and weak touchdown in open field south of Perico. No other damage was noted.

This tornado produced minor shingle damage to a home near Boyd and Sterling street on the north side of Borger along with large tree branches down. It is unclear where the tornado initially began, but there was video to suggest it touched down somewhere|over the Phillips Country Club. Additional video indicates it then moved into a small industrial site north of the homes where it dissipated. The estimated maximum wind speed was 80mph.
The tornado touched down in rural southwest Dallam County and it destroyed a barn south of FM 1727. The estimated maximum wind speed was 95mph.
Perryton AWOS measured peak wind gust of 75 mph with thunderstorms.
The mesonet located two miles north of Stinnett was hit by an outflow from a thunderstorm that was located well to the north to northeast.
Miami mesonet began having severe level wind gusts at 119 AM CDT with a peak gust of 90 mph. Severe gusts ended at 130 AM.
A large tree was blown down in the front yard of a residence. Multiple trees were blown down in the area.
A few intermittent wind gusts occurred around 60 mph in the 15 minutes before the 82 mph wind gust occurred.
A collapsing thunderstorm brought damaging winds to locations northeast of Howardwick. Irrigation pivots were blown over and a barn was damaged. Tree branches were also snapped and torn off of trees.
The walls of a farm storage building were blown down and the metal roofing blown off. Nearby tree branches were broken off. About three power poles were broken as well.
There were some locations where three to five inches of moving water accumulated on the road. Other isolated spots had one to two inches. Ditches were full in several spots and fields were flooded.
Hail fell around Vega. Most of the hailstones were quarter size but a few were up to golfball size.

Widespread wind damage occurred as a supercell moved from just west of Canyon and through Canyon. This damage consisted of snapped large and healthy tree branches , at least one uprooted tree, major roof damage, structural damage to an old outbuilding, blown over farm equipment, campers  and high profile vehicles, and at least ten snapped power poles. There was also a measured wind gust of 84 mph at the mesonet site located one mile west of Canyon.
First severe wind gust occurred at 1813 CDT and last severe wind gust occurred at 1815 CDT at the mesonet site two miles north of Texline.
The first severe wind gust occurred at 2007CDT. The peak gust of 61mph occurred at 2012 CDT at the mesonet site located 12 miles southwest of Dalhart.

Heavy rain resulted in flooding across northern Amarillo. Two cars were stalled at a low water crossing near Jason Avenue and  Oak Drive It appeared that water was roughly about six to eight inches deep at this location. Water also flooded the parking lot of David's Mexican restaurant on Hastings Avenue, where water depth was around six to eight inches deep.
The first 58 mph or greater gust occurred at 1115 AM. The peak gust of 68mph occurred at 212 PM. The final gust occurred at 216 PM.
An estimated inch of snow fell in portions of Beaver county around Beaver and just north of Floris. There was at least one wreck around Beaver due to snow impacts.
An estimated one and a half to two inches of snow fell in from Guymon to Hooker.
Several large tree branches were broken in the Westgate Mall parking lot as well as along Coulter Road.

The outer extent of the EF2 tornado that occurred southeast of Spearman also produced wind damage. This was likely caused by very strong winds associated with the rear flank downdraft of the supercell rather than the tornado itself. About two power poles were broken and a few others were leaning from the strong winds. An irrigation pivot was also turned over.
Highway 207 in Panhandle was closed with two feet of water that accumulated under the overpass.
Irrigation pivots were flipped over by the winds.

Severe wind gusts occurred at the Dalhart 12SW mesonet site from a likely anvil gust  from a nearby thunderstorm. The mesonet site  initially gusted to 61mph at 1949CDT, had its peak gust of 86mph at 1950CDT, and continued to gust to 79mph and 74mph through 1952CDT.
Severe wind gusts started at 2017CDT and continued through 2037CDT with peak wind gust of 64mph occurring at 2031CDT.
An outflow boundary moved through the mesonet site located six miles west-southwest of Adrian and produced a wind gust of 58mph.

Strong winds and hail occurred over large area just west of Dalhart to the state line,             generally extending from around Highway 87 to Highway 54. This impacted many farms and there was damage to crops throughout the area. This included some fields that were completely flattened and were a total loss.
A power pole was blown down and multiple large tree branches were snapped across the town.
Hail fell on both sides of Knowles. The west side of town had up to nickel size hail while the east side of town observed hail up to quarter size.
Four to five inch tree limbs were blown down as well as corn stalks blown completely over.
Irrigation pivots were blown over and tree damage occurred in Gate.
The mesonet site located eight miles to the west of Slapout recorded wind gusts of 58mph to 59mph from 2100CDT to 2115CDT.

A local radio station reported wind damage to the Activity Center which had its roof partially blown off. There were also some cracked windows to the center and the vents were bent. Also...one of the County Commissioners had the windows of his vehicle completely blown out which was parked two and a half blocks northwest of the Activity Center. The time of the wind damage was estimated...but reportedly occurred just before 1600 CST. No injuries were reported.
The Texas County Emergency Manager reported that high winds from a thunderstorm blew down a power pole in Guymon. No injuries were reported.

The Beaver County Emergency Manager reported thunderstorm wind damage to a home four miles south on U.S. Highway 83 at the Oklahoma and Kansas state line...and then three miles to the east and then one quarter of a mile to the north. Damage was reported to be on the north and west sides of the home. No injuries were reported.
The hail was reported near Loop 335 and Texas State Highway 136.
The Federal Aviation Administration contract weather observer at the tower reported the hail.
An off-duty National Weather Service employee estimated the thunderstorm wind gust.
An off-duty National Weather Service employee reported the hail.
An off-duty National Weather Service employee estimated the thunderstorm wind gust.
Amateur radio operators reported multiple road signs blown down with all signs laying to the west near Interstate 40 and Pullman Road. No injuries were reported.
A trained spotter reported the hail near the intersection of Farm to Market Road 1541 and Texas State Highway 217.
Thunderstorm winds reportedly blew the tin roof off of a small building and two to three inch diameter tree limbs were broken off.
A trained spotter estimated the wind gust from Sunday Canyon near the Palo Duro Canyon State Park.

Half dollar size hail fell about three miles east of Wellington. Numerous tree limbs were also blown down due to wind. However, the hail was more destructive about a mile to the southeast where a cotton field was completely destroyed.

Downburst winds occurred near and three miles north of Felt. Windows were blown out of two cars in Felt. The roofs of a feed lot three miles north of Felt and at surrounding houses were torn but not completely ripped off. Six power poles were knocked down and some were completely snapped. Small trees were snapped in two and large trees had branches snapped off. A few irrigation pivots were knocked over and broken. A stop sign was uprooted and tossed 300 feet north-northeast of its original location. All of this damage supports a downburst with winds likely over 80mph.
The mesonet site located eleven miles to the northeast of Eva recorded a severe wind gust at 1535 CDT and the final wind gust at 1545 CDT. The peak wind gust was 67mph which occurred at 1540 CDT.

Large hail fell northwest of Higgins. Hail sizes were mostly dime size to quarter size, but a few hailstones were slightly larger than a golf ball. This resulted in damage to a fire engine that was en route to a wildfire caused by lightning.
Hail up to quarter size fell for around five minutes.
Two semi trucks were blown over at the rest stop on Highway 287 south of Dumas.
The mesonet site located three miles southeast of Dumas measured two severe wind gusts in consecutive minutes. The first was 71mph at 2312 CDT and the second was 61mph at 2313CDT.
The mesonet site located six miles northeast of Pantex recorded a wind gusts of 81mph at 0028CDT. The first severe wind gust was 63mph at 0025CDT.
The mesonet site located three miles southeast of Pantex measured wind gusts between 58 and 69 mph from 0034CDT to 0043CDT with the peak gust of 69 mph which occurred at 0035CDT.
A few power poles were knocked down or snapped by the wind. Also, an irrigation pivot was knocked over and multiple large tree branches were also snapped in the area.

The mesonet station located eight miles west of Slapout measured a gust of 60 mph at 1655CDT, then measured a gust of 71 mph at 1710CDT. The final severe wind gust occurred at 1715 CDT which was 63mph.
Strong thunderstorm winds estimated around 75-80 mph violently shook and pivoted a  medium sized camper trailer, turning it about 30 degrees, with the jack stands underneath folding.
Thunderstorm winds caused damage to a barn roof. Part of the roof was removed and  hung off the side.
A trained spotter reported the hail near Farm to Market Road 1541 and slightly east of Interstate 27.
A potential heat burst occurred with weak thunderstorms nearby. The first severe wind gust occurred at 0129CDT, followed by two more severe wind gusts at 0138CDT and 0139CDT.

Three vehicles in a 100 yard area had their windows damaged by the wind or flying debris carried by the wind. Multiple tree limbs, with two as large as 8 inches in diameter, were also blown down. This occurred near the campus of Oklahoma Panhandle State University.

Heavy rainfall and multiple rounds of rain brought flash flooding to north central Randall County. Vehicles were stalled in the fast moving flood waters near the US-87 and I-27 interchange. Some roads were also closed across the city of Canyon.
One to two feet of water occurred over some bridges in Palo Duro Canyon State Park with roads being closed. Campsites were evacuated.

Heavy rainfall and multiple rounds of rain resulted in flash flooding across the city of Amarillo. There were multiple stalled vehicles in fast moving flood waters, especially across low lying areas in the roads, across Amarillo. Multiple roads were closed due to flash flood conditions.

A 58 mph wind gust was observed at the mesonet site located eleven miles to the northeast of Eva. This was associated with decaying showers. The temperature and dewpoint readings leading up to the wind gust suggested that a very small heat burst may have occurred as well.
The mesonet site located four miles south-southwest of Pantex measured wind gusts between 58 and 66 mph from 0034CDT to 0042CDT with the peak gust of 65 mph which occurred at 0038CDT.
Seven inches of standing water occurred in the roadway with at least one car stalled in the water.
Police blocked off the underpass on I-40 at the Ross Osage exit due to a car stranded and partially submerged in flood waters.
Hail fell that was mostly pea-sized but there were some nickel and quarter size hailstones that mixed in.
This wind gust was most likely caused by virga showers as winds gusted from the west-southwest with the only near by thunderstorm located to the northeast.
Hail fell to the east of Dalhart. The sizes were mostly nickel-sized but there were some hailstones the size of golf balls mixed in as well.

Large hail fell associated with a slow moving supercell just to the east of Perryton. Hail sizes ranged from 1.5 to 3.5 in diameter with this storm. At least one report of a damaged windshield was received.
Golfball to tennis ball sized hail fell.
Tennis ball to baseball size hail fell around Lefors. At least one car windshield was destroyed.
Quarter size hail fell along I-40 north of Claude.
Nickel size hail fell near the intersection of Highway 136 and Bertrand Road.
One to four inch tree limbs were snapped north of the elementary school.
A 59mph wind gust was measured at the mesonet site located nine miles north-northeast of Amarillo.
Highway 207 between Conway and Claude was closed due to three feet of water over the  highway.
A supercell thunderstorm moved across Texline and brought large hail of 2.25 inches to 2.5 inches across the city.

The Ranger Road fire ignited during the morning of February 17th near Highway 64, one mile southeast of Beaver, Oklahoma. This fire burned 283,283 acres across Oklahoma and Kansas. The fire was fueled by dormant, dry grasses and brush, driven by wind gusts of 60-70 mph and extremely low humidity (10-15%). These conditions created a fast fire environment, allowing the blaze to explode in size���growing from ignition to 15,000 acres in one hour to over 145,000 acres in just nine hours. It rapidly crossed the state line into Clark, Comanche, and Meade counties in Kansas. With strong wind gusts, this helped not only to spread the fire but limited aerial firefighting operations and complicated suppression efforts during the first stages of the fire's expansion. The cause is undetermined.  A firefighter was injured from being burned. In addition, a fire truck from Rosston Fire overturned in Beaver County and three fire fighters were injured, including one that suffered from 2nd and 3rd degree burns and broke his leg. There were 926 primary homes, 2 schools, and commercial/government buildings threatened. Evacuations: Mandatory evacuations for about 771 people that may have covered KS as well.  Gate and Knowles had evacuations on Feb 17th, and numerous outbuildings were destroyed in the fire.

The Stevens Fire ignited around 11:45 a.m. on February 17, 2026, approximately seven miles northwest of Hooker, Oklahoma, in Texas County. The fire burned 12,894 acres and was caused by human activities. Smoke from this fire reduced visibility along US Highway 54, which resulted in a seven vehicle accident and additional fire start(which became the Side Road Fire). Mandatory evacuations occurred for the town of Tyrone on the 17th and were lifted by the morning of February 21st. US Highway 54 was closed between Tyrone and Hooker due to smoke and fire activity.  Five structures were burned: 4 barns and one house per OEMA. About 263 homes were threatened by this fire.

The Side Road Fire ignited on the afternoon of February 17, 2026, in Texas County, Oklahoma as a result of dry fuels, low humidity and wind gusts exceeding 60mph. The fire started near U.S. Highway 54, approximately 5 miles west of Tyrone and north of Guymon. This fire started as the result of a seven car accident that occurred on as a result of poor visibility from smoke from the nearby Stevens Fire. The Side Road fire burned 3680 acres. Mandatory evacuations were issued for the community of Tyrone and surrounding areas on February 17th and were lifted on February 21st, and US Highway 54 was closed between Hooker and Tyrone during the height of the fire due to smoke and emergency equipment.  At least six homes were destroyed off Highway 56 and Road D.

The Morning Fire burned 820 acres.  It started near Highway 83 and County Road 21, about nine miles northwest of Balko. This fire occurred as a result of a car accident that occurred just after 9am on February 19th.

The 8 Ball Fire ignited on February 17, 2026, approximately 12 miles west of Clarendon, or ten miles west of Howardwick, along the US 287 corridor in Armstrong County. The fire was fueled by freeze-cured tall grasses and brush, driven by critical fire weather conditions including wind gusts up to 45 mph and low humidity. It exhibited rapid growth initially, spreading from a reported 200 acres to thousands of acres within the first 24 hours. Forward progress of the fire was stopped on the evening of February 18th but was contained on February 21st. In total, Eight Ball Fire burned 13563 acres across Armstrong and Donley counties.  There were evacuations in the Howardwick area on February 17th, which were lifted later on February 18th. US Highway 287 was closed from Goodnight to Ashtola for a couple of hours. Highway 70 was also briefly closed. The fire threatened approximately 1,100 homes and critical infrastructure. At the peak of the event, roughly 400 homes were evacuated.  The cause of the fire is human related with a connection to passenger vehicle or motorized RV usage.

The Lavender Fire ignited on February 17, 2026, approximately five miles south of Boys Ranch in Oldham County. The fire began along the U.S. Highway 385 corridor. The fire was fueled by critically dry, waist-high grass and extreme wind conditions. It exhibited rapid growth initially, pushed by strong west winds with gusts reaching 50-60 mph. The fire quickly crossed key roadways, including FM 1061 (Tascosa Road), and spread toward the Canadian River. In total, the Lavender Fire burned 18423 acres across Oldham County and into Potter County.  Mandatory evacuations were issued for the Valley De Oro community and areas between Tascosa Road (FM 1061) and U.S. Highway 287 in north-central Potter County during the afternoon of February 17th. The Ady neighborhood was also evacuated on February 18th. FM 1061(Tascosa Road) at US Highway 385/281 was closed due to fires during the afternoon of February 17th and was reopened during the evening of February 18th. The Texas Department of Public Safety also shutdown Highway 287 on February 17th and US 87 was closed in both directions from FM 1719, just north of Amarillo to SH 354, south of Dumas. Approximately 250 people and homes were affected.  Incident report noted 40 homes saved, and 7 homes lost. In addition, Xcel Energy implemented a Public Safety Power Shutoff (PSPS) to reduce wildfire risk, which affected thousands of customers and resulted in some schools closing for the day due to lack of electricity and ability to feed students. The cause of the fire is undetermined.
The Canadian River Bridge Fire occurred about five miles north of Borger, just off of Highway 136 at the Canadian River. This fire burned 428 acres and was caused by welding equipment use.

The Flat Tire wildfire ignited at approximately 11:35 a.m. on February 10, 2026, in Beaver County, Oklahoma. The fire was located south of the town of Turpin, or 1/4 of a mile east of the intersection NS123 and EW10. It burned in and around the Beaver River bottom area. This fire was human caused. Officials noted that a flat tire had blown off and sparked, which caused the ignition. The fire was fueled by exceptional fuel loading in the county. The fire burned 1,983 acres. No damage to homes or major structures occurred with this fire. However, US Highway 83 was closed on February 10th in Turpin to US Highway 412 due to the fire.

The No Tire wildfire started nearly the same location as the Flat Tire fire occurred.  It started further down the road as the car that ignited the Flat Tire fire continued to travel on the rim with no tire attached, and the rim would go on to set a new separate ignition point than the Flat Tire did. This fire was located one quarter of a mile west of the intersection of NS122 and EW10. This fire burned 331 acres.

The Willard Fire ignited on February 24, 2026, in Dallam County.  The fire occurred near Willard Lane and Farm to Market Road 807. This is located about ten miles southwest of Stratford. This fire burned 540 acres. The cause of the fire is unknown as the origin of it was destroyed according to fire department reports. It did threaten one home and one structure.

Drought conditions worsened across the Oklahoma Panhandle during the month. The month began with the region mostly in Moderate Drought (D1), except for a small area of Abnormally Dry (D0) conditions in northern Cimarron County. Within the first ten days, Severe Drought (D2) expanded to cover the majority of Beaver County. By day 17, two-thirds of Cimarron County, particularly the southwest portion, had also reached D2. By day 24, D2 conditions covered the entire Panhandle, excluding the southeast corner of Beaver County. Furthermore, an area of Extreme Drought (D3) had developed over central Beaver County. Precipitation deficits over the past 120 days, which were already 1 to 2 inches below normal, increased by an additional 1 to 2 inches.

At that point, the drought intensified, with Dallam, Hartley, Sherman, and Moore Counties all escalating to Severe Drought (D2). This transition was marked by an additional 1 to 2 being added to the existing 120-day precipitation deficit. Furthermore, the severity of the drought's impact on winter crops was worsened by record monthly maximum temperatures recorded during the month.

The Lavender Fire ignited on February 17, 2026, approximately five miles south of Boys Ranch in Oldham County. The fire began along the U.S. Highway 385 corridor. The fire was fueled by critically dry, waist-high grass and extreme wind conditions. It exhibited rapid growth initially, pushed by strong west winds with gusts reaching 50-60 mph. The fire quickly crossed key roadways, including FM 1061 (Tascosa Road), and spread toward the Canadian River. In total, the Lavender Fire burned 18423 acres across Oldham County and into Potter County.  Mandatory evacuations were issued for the Valley De Oro community and areas between Tascosa Road (FM 1061) and U.S. Highway 287 in north-central Potter County during the afternoon of February 17th. The Ady neighborhood was also evacuated on February 18th. FM 1061(Tascosa Road) at US Highway 385/281 was closed due to fires during the afternoon of February 17th and was reopened during the evening of February 18th. The Texas Department of Public Safety also shutdown Highway 287 on February 17th and US 87 was closed in both directions from FM 1719, just north of Amarillo to SH 354, south of Dumas. Approximately 250 people and homes were affected.  Incident report noted 40 homes saved, and 7 homes lost. In addition, Xcel Energy implemented a Public Safety Power Shutoff (PSPS) to reduce wildfire risk, which affected thousands of customers and resulted in some schools closing for the day due to lack of electricity and ability to feed students. The cause of the fire is undetermined.

The 8 Ball Fire ignited on February 17, 2026, approximately 12 miles west of Clarendon, or ten miles west of Howardwick, along the US 287 corridor in Armstrong County. The fire was fueled by freeze-cured tall grasses and brush, driven by critical fire weather conditions including wind gusts up to 45 mph and low humidity. It exhibited rapid growth initially, spreading from a reported 200 acres to thousands of acres within the first 24 hours. Forward progress of the fire was stopped on the evening of February 18th but was contained on February 21st. In total, Eight Ball Fire burned 13563 acres across Armstrong and Donley counties.  There were evacuations in the Howardwick area on February 17th, which were lifted later on February 18th. US Highway 287 was closed from Goodnight to Ashtola for a couple of hours. Highway 70 was also briefly closed. The fire threatened approximately 1,100 homes and critical infrastructure. At the peak of the event, roughly 400 homes were evacuated.  The cause of the fire is unknown.

The Hutchinson Fire sparked on March 24th shortly before noon and ignited about 2.5 northeast of Sanford Texas.  The fire was human caused and believed to be connected to an electrical transmission distribution system. The fire would go on to burn about 2,937 acres.  This would also take about 3 days to contain. Over the course of 3 days it managed to burn 2,937 acres.  Additionally, mandatory evacuations were ordered for Sanford and parts of Stinnett on March 24th.  The fire was burning in an area of difficult terrain to manage which lead to a longer burn period to get it under control.  Since the fire was difficult to control on day one, critical fire weather on both the 25th and 26th didn't help at all as temperatures were near 100 degrees both days with breezy winds and low humidity.  Add the difficult terrain to the mix, and it made for a challenge to get the fire under control.

This fire, named the Unity Corner fire, started from human-related activities during the afternoon hours of March 5th at Mile 20 & Road Q, northwest of Guymon.  It burned 312 acres and was contained within about eight hours with minimal impact to communities and homes.

Drought conditions worsened across the Oklahoma Panhandle during the month. The month began with the region in Severe Drought (D2) but much of Beaver County was encompassed in Extreme Drought (D3).  The region continued to see a lack of significant rainfall during the month, with Beaver County seeing more rainfall than the rest of the Oklahoma Panhandle during the month. Rainfall amounts of around 0.2 inches to 0.7 inches fell during the month. However, Beaver County ended April with precipitation deficits of around 1.3-1.8 inches, with a very localized exception in the far northwest part of the county where deficits were around 0.4 inches. Precipitation deficits over the past 120 days were 3.5 inches to 4.5 inches and near 5 inches in the far southern part of the county.

The month began with the region in Severe Drought (D2) but by around the 21st of the month, Extreme Drought (D3) expanded into much of Texas County from the west.  The region continued to see a lack of significant rainfall during the month. Rainfall amounts of around 0.2 inches to 0.8 inches fell during the month. However, Texas County ended April with precipitation deficits of around 0.75 to 1.2 inches. Precipitation deficits over the past 120 days were 2.75 to 3.3 inches. This lack of rainfall contributed to dry fuels in the region and when dry thunderstorms moved over the area, some wildfires were sparked from the lightning.

Texas A&M Forest Service noted that this originated in Swisher County, but the fire still spread to Armstrong County.  Cause Unknown.  Acres burnt 1,300.  Two homes were saved, but unfortunately one home was lost. This fire was called Dolly wildfire.

Critical fire weather conditions occurred in Oldham County on March 8th as observed relative humidity values were around 6% at the Vega West Texas Mesonet. RFTIs of 5-8 were observed for nearly 6 hours that afternoon. The Maroon fire was sparked due to a passenger motorized RV. The fire was contained morning of March 9th with the total area burned being 745 acres. The fire did cause US Highway 385 to be closed between Channing and Boys Ranch for a period of time.

On March 9th critical Fire Weather conditions occurred for several hours across Gray County. A wildfire was sparked 4 miles southeast of Lefors. The fire was known as the Cabin Creek Fire. The fire caused closures on several FM/SH roads. A few structures were threatened and saved as well as some oil and gas infrastructure. The final size of the fire was 6,949 acres. The cause of the fire was unknown. Cabin Creek Fire. The cause of the fire is believed to be human, from a passenger vehicle. But this fire did burn 6,949 acres.

On March 10th, a high based thunderstorm with dry lightning ignited a wildfire in far southwest Moore County. The fire, which would be named Yellow Fire, sparked around 6:30pm and occurred near the border of Moore, Oldham and Hartley counties. Gusty, erratic winds occurred at the Boys Ranch mesonet around that time, and while relative humidity values were around 20%, the winds and the critically dry fuels allowed for rapid wildfire growth. The wildfire was estimated to have burned 14,374 acres and was contained on March 13th. East and westbound SH 354 was temporarily closed from US Highway 385 to US Highway 87 from March 10th through early on the 11th. Additional roads also experienced at least temporary closures such as RM 1061 at FM 281 and Highway 385. There was also a voluntary evacuation of Valley de Oro and an evacuation of the Boys Ranch community.

On March 10th a fire sparked about 5 miles southwest of Canadian Texas known as the Little Fire. The fire was believed to be caused by a motorized vehicle due to roadside activity. The fire managed to burn 401 acres and was contained by March 11th. The fire weather conditions were just elevated that day as winds were on the lighter side when the fire ignited, they did pick up in the 10 to 20 mph range with RH values around 25 to 35 percent, so elevated fire weather conditions at best were observed. Not much on this fire other than it was a roadside fire that burned about 401 acres in Hemphill County.

Although we had elevated Fire Weather conditions on March 15th, the winds were still consistently in the 20 to 30 mph range through the afternoon. And with the fuels still critically dry across the Panhandles it wouldn't be hard for a wildfire to spark and be hard to control. While it's unknown how the fire started, we ended up getting the Neon Beige Fire in Oldham County. This fire would go on to burn about 1688 acres. The fire caused US highway 385 to be closed from Tascosa to Vega due to heavy smoke .  While the Neon Beige fire's cause was unknown, it did have some impacts like closing HWY 385 from Vega to Tascosa for a period of time, and it managed to burn 1688 acres.

On March 15th we had critical fire weather conditions, but it wasn't your typical fire weather day. We had strong north winds that had frequent gusts over 50 mph and some gusts got up to 60 mph near the fire area. While temperatures were cool, in the 50s the RH values were still on the lower side below 30 percent and with the dry grasses due to lack of soil moisture, any fire that ignited in these conditions would still be able to spread quickly. While this fire was contained at just 234 acres, it did trigger mandatory evacuations on the south side of Greenbelt Lake where about 340 homes were evacuated, and overall the fire threatened over 2,100 homes in the surrounding area. The Corner Pocket fire while smaller than usual for documentation, did manage to require several homes to be evacuated. It's believed to be human caused by power generator, and managed to burn 234 acres.
The North Twin Fire was reported around 12:30 pm CDT about 2 miles northeast of Bugbee, TX. The fire is believed to be human caused by a vehicle.  The fire would go on to burn 518 acres.

The South Twin fire ignited 2 miles northwest of Sanford, TX and would go on to burn 365 acres.  The cause of the fire was unknown.  Both North and South Twin fires were noted as contained by the evening of the 5th.

A fire ignited about 17 miles north of Amarillo along Highway 287, it was known as the Meadow View fire and it would go on to burn 1262 acres before being contained a couple days later.  The cause of the fire was unknown.  Fire weather conditions that day were elevated to critical at times.  Winds were 20-25 mph with RH values down around 15 percent.

There is not much information on the Mary 15 Wildfire, but from what we can see it occurred 17 miles NW of Guymon, OK and it burned 899 acres.  It's cause was natural, and it was updated as contained on the morning of April 12th.

The Lightning Roll Wildfire was caused by dry lightning on the evening of April 9th and would go on to burn 2412 acres.  While we don't have full containment date on record, it was updated as over 70 percent contained by the morning of April 12th.

Dry and windy conditions occurred on April 9th.  The Smooth Eddy wildfire resulted under these conditions, but we do not know how the fire started.  But the conditions were favorable for quick wildfire growth. No other significant factors were noted on this wildfire.  The wildfire would go on to burn 552 acres.

Purple Monster wildfire sparked the evening of April 9th about 9 miles north of Vega, TX due to dry lightning.  Gusty winds out of the thunderstorm would aid in the fire spread, as well as critically dry fuels and still low overall RH values. Part of the fire was on rugged and would be a challenge to tackle, and the fire would go on to burn 1911 acres before being contained.

The Paper Wings wildfire ignited due to dry lightning and burned 439 acres. Prior to the dry lightning we had several hours of critical Fire Weather that started around 1 in the afternoon.  So add that to the dry fuels and it makes for easy ignition from either humans or lightning.

The Horny Toad wildfire would go on to burn 680 acres.  Elevated to near critical fire weather conditions were present on April 12th as winds in the afternoon did range from 20 to 25 mph and RH values dropped into the mid teens.  This along with our critically dry fuels allowed for any fires that started to spread quickly.
The Pump Jack wildfire ignited the evening of the 18th and would go on to burn 300 acres.  The cause of this fire is unknown.

The Smartside wildfire burned about 71 acres in northeast Amarillo.  Fire Warnings were issued due to the fire threatening a community on the northeast side of town.  Travis Intermediate School was evacuated due to the fire.
