This was the first of two tornadoes produced by this supercell. The most significant damage was to a sturdy steel constructed outbuilding which was completely destroyed. Damage to a nearby home included broken windows, removal of roof decking material and uplifting of the roof. 2 by 4 pieces of wood were embedded in the roof of the house. A large flat bed truck was moved 50 yards. This tornado was rated EF-2 with an estimated peak wind of 115 mph. The tornado continued into Gray County.

This was the first of two tornadoes produced by this supercell. The most significant damage occurred in Carson County which caused the tornado to be rated EF-2 with an estimated peak wind of 115 mph. The tornado ended shortly after crossing into Gray County.

This tornado was produced by the second supercell thunderstorm to impact the Pampa area and the same storm which resulted in the Groom tornado. The most significant damage was to the Halliburton Plant just east of Pampa. Sturdy commercial steel framed building at the Halliburton Plant were completely leveled with nmerous vehicles tossed on top of the rubble. This tornado was less than 3 miles from directly hitting the city of Pampa. One manufactured home was completely destroyed south of Pampa. This tornado was rated EF-3 with maximum winds estimated to be 155 mph based on the degree of damage.

This long track tornado caused damage mainly to power lines and trees due to its rural track. It was the first tornado to pass near Pampa. Some trees were debarked and completely defoliated leaving only the trunks. The collapse of a high tension power line metal truss tower is the basis for the EF-3 rating. Maximum winds were estimated to be 140 mph. The tornado continued into Roberts County.

This long track tornado moved into Roberts County from Gray County and caused damage mainly to power lines and trees due to its rural track. It was the first tornado to pass near Pampa. Some trees were debarked and completely defoliated leaving only the trunks. The collapse of a high tension power line metal truss tower is the basis for the EF-3 rating. Maximum winds were estimated to be 140 mph.

The details of this tornado track was primarily based on video and photo evidence, and radar data. This tornado was produced by the same supercell which caused the tornado near Groom and the tornado near Pampa which destroyed the Halliburton Plant. Damage from this particular tornado was limited to broken wooden utility poles in Roberts County. The tornado was rated EF-1 with an estimated maximum wind speed of 100 mph. The tornado continued from Gray County into Roberts County.

Much of the track of this storm was across farmland which was inaccessible. Therefore, track width and tornado strengths are based on locations where it crossed roadways. One home sustained roof damage. Additional damage included trees, fences, metal sheds, and oil field equipment. A rating of EF-1 was assigned wit estimated maximum winds of 90 mph. The tornado started in northern Hemphill County and continued through Lipscomb County and into Ellis County, Oklahoma.

Wind gusts as high as 65 mph were recorded at the West Texas Mesonet site near Hereford just before 8:00 PM CST on the 26th. This preceded the snowfall which began a few hours later. The first report from Deaf Smith County was received at around 6:00 AM on the 27th of 3 inches of snow accumulation with 4 to 5 foot drifts. Later on the morning of the 27th it was reported that several roads in Hereford were impassible and several vehicles were stranded, with less than one quarter mile visibility due to blowing snow. Storm total snowfall amounts from across the county include: 10 inches in Bootleg; 4 inches in Hereford with; 5 inches in Dawn. This equals the 3rd largest daily accumulation for the nearest climate station in Hereford, TX where records go back to 1905. These amounts do not adequately describe conditions however, as very strong winds produced very large snow drifts in the area further amplifying impacts to much greater levels than typically associated with a 10 inch snowfall event. 4 to 6 foot drifts were common across the county with some locations receiving drifts up to 10 feet deep.

Total snowfall accumulation ranged from 1.5 to 2 inches across the county. Blizzard conditions existed due to strong winds and reduced visibility from blowing snow. Visibility was lower than one quarter mile for a period. The strong winds also caused significant drifting of snow. A peak wind gust of 69 mph was measured by the Automated Surface Observing System at the Dalhart Airport.

This was the first of two tornadoes that developed from the same supercell near Howardwick. The tornado motion was somewhat unusual as it moved toward the west. This tornado moved across open fields. The only damage was to a pivot irrigation system. Damage was consistent with EF-0 with estimated peak winds of 80 mph.

This was the second tornado from this supercell. The tornado was well documented by chasers as it moved around the main storm rotation creating a U-shaped track which was perpendicular to the storm motion at times. The tornado destroyed a barn, damaged power lines and two large sections of pivot irrigation as it narrowly missed a farm house. The tornado stalled at the end of the track and become an impressive multi-vortex tornado which stayed in nearly the same location for several minutes. The damage was consistent with EF-1 damage, with estimated peak winds 100 mph, however it should be noted the tornado did not hit any targets that would allow for a higher rating.

This tornado snapped trees, damaged power lines and flipped pivot irrigation systems. This large tornado was briefly visible in the background of storm chaser video of the tornado to the southwest as it dissipated. Once again, this tornado occurred in an area with few targets, but what damage that did occur was consistent with EF-1 with estimated peak winds of 95 mph.

Damage from this tornado included snapped tree trunks, damaged power poles, and flipped pivot irrigation systems. This damage is consistent with EF-1, with peak winds of 95 mph although few targets where hit. Similar to other tornadoes with this event, the track exhibited significant curvature following a counter-clockwise path.

The tornado began just west of Highway 136 in extreme eastern Potter County. Storm chasers witnessed the tornado form and cross the highway. One power pole was snapped along Highway 136 which was consistent with EF1 Damage. The tornado then continued into Carson County and produced damage just across the county line which was consistent with EF-2 on the Fujita Tornado Damage Scale. This damage occurred along County Road 1342 where a well anchored double wide mobile home was completely rolled and damaged. The tornado continued east and moved to near County Road C before dissipating.

Two separate microbursts were observed with thunderstorms in the Skellytown and Pampa areas on Saturday evening. A significant downburst wind event occurred west and southwest of Dalhart, TX on Sunday evening. The downburst was associated with an RFD of a supercell thunderstorm. Damage from the downburst was initially observed at the Twisted Elms Golf Course were several trees were uprooted and many large branches were downed, including some onto power lines. Damage at the golf course was estimated at 75-85 MPH. The damage continued to the southeast were several power poles were blown down. Severe straight line damaged peaked at the airport where a 74 MPH wind was observed with even some of NWS ASOS equipment was damaged afterwards by flying debris from airport hangers up to half a mile away. Several small planes and a pop-up camper were flipped and thrown up to 50 yards. Damage at the airport was estimated to be from 100 to 110 MPH winds, which is equivalent of a high end EF-1 tornado.

Given a rainfall shortfall that began in July, a small area of severe drought (D2) began early in November in the northwest part of Texas County per the U.S. Drought Monitor.  By the end of the month, this area spread south and east, eventually including about the northwest one-fourth of Texas County. Fall grazing was impacted, and ranchers were required to bring in food for cattle.

Given a rainfall shortfall that began in July, an area of severe drought (D2) became established by the third week of November in the northeast and north-central part of Cimarron County per the U.S. Drought Monitor.  By the end of the month, this area spread south and east, eventually including all but the extreme southeast and south-central parts  of Cimarron County. Fall grazing was impacted, and ranchers were required to bring in food for cattle. Red winter wheat was greatly affected during planting, with much of the non-irrigated wheat not taking root.

High winds caused blowing dust which reduced visibility to near zero. These conditions contributed to a traffic crash on U.S. Highway 54 around 1440CST around 11 miles northeast of Stratford involving a northeast-bound tractor-trailer driver who was unable to see the highway markings, became disoriented, and locked up the vehicle's brakes when it crossed center stripe causing a head-on collision. This vehicle collided head-on with a southwest-bound tractor-trailer in the left passing lane. The driver of a third tractor-trailer, which was southwest-bound in the right lane, in an attempt to avoid the collision, struck the other southwest-bound vehicle. The driver and passenger of the third vehicle were able to get out of the truck tractor before it became fully engulfed in flames. The drivers of the first two vehicles died at the scene. According to the nearest mesonet station, northwest winds of 40 to 47 MPH with gusts up to 60 MPH were occurring at the time of the accident.

While some pockets of 2-3 inch monthly rainfall total occurred, many areas received less than 1 inch in June and this followed several months of below normal rainfall. The county-wide area of severe drought (D2) at the end of May was overtaken by a large area of extreme drought (D3) which emerged over the northwestern three-fourths of the county in the first week of June. By the second week of June extreme drought encompassed all but the far southeast part of the county. Winter Wheat was in the process of being harvested and rates were around 9-10 bushels per acre when they should be closer to 40. Grazing grasslands had been completely depleted and cattle were being sold off. Dry conditions led to several small lightning induced wildfires on multiple occasions in the area when thunderstorms did form.

The area severe drought (D2) which covered the northwest one-third of the county at the end of May expanded southeast to include of the county during the second week of June. Areas of extreme drought (D3) emerged in the second week of June over far northwest and southeast parts of the county. These areas of extreme drought persisted for the rest of the month, with the far northeast part of the county also going into extreme drought during the last week of the month. Dry-land crops were adversely affected by drought and it was estimated that no attempt was made to plant 12,000 to 13,000 acres of milo given extreme soil dryness. Many dry-land (non-irrigated) fields that were planted failed. The county relaxed rules for utilizing Conservation Reserve Program (CRP) lands as an emergency measure and allowed use without cost to farmers and also allowed 100% hay harvest if requested. Some cattle were reportedly sold off as a result of sparse grazing. Dry conditions led to several small lightning induced wildfires on multiple occasions in the area when thunderstorms did form.

An area of severe drought (D2) emerged during the second week of the month in the far southwest part of the county. By the end of the month, this area had spread east to include roughly the western half of the county. Also, during the final week of the month, a small area of extreme drought (D3) emerged in the far northwest part of the county.

The area severe drought (D2) which covered all but the far southeast and east-central parts of the county at the end of May expanded southeast to include all of the county during the second week of June. Also, during the second week of the month, the northwest two-thirds of the county went into extreme drought (D3), with further southeastward expansion of extreme drought occurring by the middle of the month, to include the northwest three-fourths of the county. Thunderstorms provided some relief during the third week of the month, so that the area of severe drought retreated from the far southeast part of the county by the end of the month. In a similar fashion, the area of extreme drought grew smaller, to include the northern one-third and the extreme southwest part of the county by the end of the month. Dry conditions caused native and pastureland grasses to return to cured status and led to a lack of available grazing for cattle.

It was reported that many cotton fields with young plants were a complete loss as the plants were sheared apart to ground level by the combination of high winds and blowing dust.

Most of the county was experiencing extreme drought (D3) early in July. Beneficial rainfall improved drought conditions in the south, although abnormally dry (D0) to moderate drought remained (D1).  Extreme drought (D3) persisted through July across the far north where less rainfall occurred.

Most of the county was experiencing severe drought (D2) while there was a portion in the northwest, northeast and southeast that were in extreme drought (D3) heading into July. There was even a very small area, probably only about 1% of the county that was in exceptional drought (D4) in the far northwest initially. Beneficial monsoon rainfall developed and increase around the third week of July and continued through the end of the month. Rainfall in Goodwell was well above normal by the end of the month with 6.77 inches of precipitation measured. Guymon's monthly precipitation came in at 5.17 inches. Most of the county had reduced its drought severity by 2 categories. By the end of the month, most of the county had improved to abnormally dry (D0) status with the area between Texhoma, Goodwell, and Guymon were completely removed from all drought categories.

The western half of Beaver County was severe drought (D2) with small areas in the northwest and southwest in extreme drought (D3) going into July. The eastern half was only in moderate drought (D1) going into the month of July. For the first part of July most of the county degraded into severe drought (D2), although the D3 in the northwest did improve with some beneficial rainfall in the beginning of the month. During the third week of July, the county started to get enough rainfall to eliminate D2 conditions across the entire county. Abnormally dry (D0) to moderate drought (D1) conditions remained with the worse conditions noted across the northwest quarter of the county as Beaver and Slapout ended the month with just under 2 inches of rainfall which is just below normal.

Armstrong County saw a little bit of rain in the first week of July allowing for a temporary reduction from severe drought (D2) to moderate drought (D1) in the southwest around the Palo Duro Canyon area. This did not last long and soon returned mid month and stayed until the end. Short to very short topsoil and subsoil moisture levels were reported.

Carson County started the month of July with severe drought (D2) to extreme drought (D3) conditions in the north to northwest, almost half, of the county. Dryland cotton was not growing in the Texas Panhandle where D2 and D3 conditions were existing. In Carson County, 90 percent of the dryland cotton did not sprout. From about the third week of July some beneficial monsoonal rains dropped 1.79 inches in Panhandle which is about average for the month. This helped erode some of the D2 and D3 conditions going into August with the exception of the far northeast corner of the county. Wells were struggling to keep up with irrigation demand. Pasture and rangeland conditions were reported as very poor to fair. Reports were made of very short to short topsoil and subsoil moisture levels. During the month of July at least one big wildfire was reported due to the dry conditions. No acreage information was available, but 9 different Fire Departments responded to contain the fire and avoid structure damage.

Extreme drought (D3) conditions dominated the south to southeast portions of the county through the first half of the month with most of the rest of the county in severe drought (D2). The most beneficial rainfall from monsoonal moisture fell during the 3rd week of the month. 1.20 inches of the 1.82 inches that fell in for Borger, occurred on the 16th, 19th, and 20th of the month. A small portion or D3 to D2 still existed in the far southeast corner of the county going into August.  In July, a couple of wildfires were started by lightning due to the dryness of vegetation. About 9000 to 10,000 acres burned from two different fires started by lightning.

Severe drought (D2) to extreme drought (D3) existed in the southwest half of the county going into the first week of July. Some beneficial monsoonal rainfall fell in the northern half of the county eroding the the D2 conditions in the portions of the northwest while D2 and D3 conditions began to appear in all of the southern areas along the county line into Gray County.  Wells were struggling to keep up with irrigation demand. Pasture and rangeland conditions were reported as very poor to fair. Reports were made of very short to short topsoil and subsoil moisture levels.

Hemphill County were not so lucky in receiving monsoonal rainfall during the month of July as some nearby counties did. Just enough rain fell to roughly maintain severe drought (D2) in the southern portion of the county while only seeing a slight improvement in the north to the moderate drought (D1) conditions.

Gray County started out the month with severe drought (D2) in the northern half to two thirds of the county. July was very dry for Gray County and extreme drought spread across the northern portions of the county. A small portion of the southern part of the county managed to stay with abnormally dry (D0) to moderate drought (D1) as just enough rainfall fell to keep conditions worsening.

Wheeler County started the month with severe drought (D2) conditions in the northern half of the county. July continued to be below normal in rainfall introducing severe drought to the entire county with some extreme drought (D3) conditions developing across the central portion of the county through the first 3 weeks of July. During the fourth week some rain fell, but it was just enough to return most of the county to severe drought with a small portion of extreme drought in the northwest corner of the county. Wells were struggling to keep up with irrigation demand. Pasture and rangeland conditions were reported as very poor to fair. Reports were made of very short to short topsoil and subsoil moisture levels.

Extreme drought (D3) existed in the far southwest of the county but quickly expanded to a majority of the southwestern portion of the county through July. Almost all of the county was in at least severe drought (D2) up until the last week of July when some beneficial rainfall helped reduce the severity of the far northern portion of the County (Amarillo northward). Range land grasses were non-existent with ranchers starting to consider selling off cattle in order to save money on feed. Hay prices were $10 to $20 higher per ton than else where in the state. Farmers were starting to consider abandoning dryland crops such as cotton and sorghum due the lack of water and seed not being able to germinate.  Short to very short topsoil and subsoil moisture levels were reported.

Extreme drought (D3) existed in the northern half of the county, as well as a small sliver in the southwest going into July. With an exception of a portion in the southeast that was in moderate drought (D1), the rest of the county was in at least severe drought (D2). Beneficial monsoonal rainfall developed early in the month with Dalhart receiving 0.85 on the 3rd of the month and 0.70 on the 4th. Texline  received around 1.30 between those two days.  This allowed the county to drop at least one category in Drought during the first week. There was a small break in the rain during week 2, then drought conditions started to improve significantly with the county ending week 3 with no areas of severe drought and week 4 with only a couple of small areas in abnormally dry. Texline received a whopping 8.82 inches for a monthly total.

About a third of Sherman County was in severe drought (D2) going into the month of July with less than one inch falling for each month previously at Stratford. Wells were struggling to keep up with irrigation demand. Pasture and rangeland conditions were reported as very poor to fair. Reports were made of very short to short topsoil and subsoil moisture levels. Beneficial monsoonal rainfall began to fall in the month of July allowing for Stratford and surrounding areas to receive 3 to 4 inches.  Severe drought was removed by the end of week 3. By the end of the month Sherman County had managed to expel all categories of drought. Around July 11, at least one wildfire was started by lightning due to the dry conditions through around mid July. This fire burned around 300 acres.

The majority of Hansford County was in severe drought (D2) going into July with a small area in extreme drought (D3) in the northeast. A portion of the southeast remained in moderate drought (D1). Like a lot of areas in the TX Panhandle the majority of beneficial monsoonal rainfall fell in the third week. Areas near Gruver received 4 to 5 inches removing all D3 and D2 drought classifications from the county. By week 4 an additional 1-2 inches of rain fell. Wells were struggling to keep up with irrigation demand. Pasture and rangeland conditions were reported as very poor to fair. Reports were made of very short to short topsoil and subsoil moisture levels.

Ochiltree County was in moderate drought (D1) through at least the first two weeks of July with a third of the county in severe drought (D2) to extreme drought (D3) mainly in the north to northwestern portions of the county. In the third week of the month three beneficial monsoonal rainfall began to improve conditions and all areas fell below severe drought status by the end of the month. Areas around Perryton ended the month with 5 to 6 inches of rainfall for July, which is near 200% of normal.

Hartley County began the month with a little over half of the western portion of the county in extremem drought (D3). The eastern portion of the county tapered off from severe drought (D2) to moderate drought (D1) further east. Wells were struggling to keep up with irrigation demand. Pasture and rangeland conditions were reported as very poor to fair. Reports were made of very short to short topsoil and subsoil moisture levels.

Much of Potter County received rainfall surpluses of 1-2 inches which was 150 to 300 percent of normal for July. While much of the county were included in severe (D2) to extreme Drought (D3) at the beginning of July, no severe drought designation remained by July 28th. Abnormally dry (D0) and moderate drought conditions did persist in southern portions of the county. With such poor conditions at the beginning of the month ranchers were having to bring in feed for cattle, with little to no grasses in pasture. Dry land crops were also not doing well and practically non-existed in the beginning of the month.

Much of Oldham County received rainfall surpluses of 1-2 inches which was 150 to 300 percent of normal for July. While much of the county were included in severe (D2) to extreme Drought (D3) at the beginign of July, no severe drought diesignation remained by July 28th. Abnomally dry (D0) and modertate drought conditions did persist in western and southern portions of the county.

Below normal rainfall from previous months already placed Collingsworth County in moderate drought (D1) going into July. By July 7th, severe drought (D2) started creeping into the northeastern portions of the county.  Severe drought continued to spread across most of the county with the exception of far western portions by the end of the month.

Deaf Smith County was in at least severe drought (D2) to extreme drought (D3) throughout the county initially. A small portion of the county in the north managed to tap into some monsoonal rainfall during the last week allowing for a temporary improvement to moderate drought (D1) going into the first week of August. Range land grasses were non-existent with ranchers considering selling off cattle in order to save money on feed. Hay prices are $10 to $20 higher per ton than else where in the state. Farmers were considering abandoning dryland crops such as cotton due the lack of water and seed not being able to germinate.  Short to very short topsoil and subsoil moisture levels were reported.

Cimarron County begin the month with much of the northwest half of the area included in extreme (D3) drought. Some late July and August rainfall did lead to slight improvement to severe drought (D2), but much of the county only received 25 to 50% of normal rainfall which added an additional 1 to 3 inch inches to the ongoing deficits.

A portion of the southwest corner of the county was in severe drought going into August. About mid-August a small area of extreme drought conditions started showing as in the southwest. One rain event at the end of August briefly improved conditions shrinking  areas of severe and extrem drought just slightly. Soil moisture has been classified and very poor to fare. Agricultural impacts have not improved through the month of August. Rain deficits remain between 6 to 12 inches year to date.  Hay prices in the TX PH were $10 to $20 higher per ton compared to the rest of the state. Range land grasses are sparse making it pricy to feed cattle. A lot of dry land crops were abandoned and non-irrigated crops did not grow.

Carson County started the month of August 1/8th corner of the county in Severe Drought (D2) with a small sliver of Extreme Drought (D3). The rest of the county was abnormally dry to moderate drought (D1). Carson County managed to receive some beneficial rainfall, around 2 to 3 inches, across much of the county allowing all D2 and D3 areas to be removed by August 29th.  Hay prices in the TX PH were $10 to $20 higher per ton compared to the rest of the state. A lot of dry land crops were abandoned and non-irrigated crops did not grow. Monsoonal rains in the latter part of July and early August helped soil moisture but it was too late for almost all dry land crops.

Collingsworth County started the month of August with a very small sliver of Severe Drought (D2) in the far southwest corner. As the weeks went on conditions worsened with D2 expanding across the entire county. Even the small sliver in the southwest corner deteriated into Extreme Drought (D3). The northwest third to half of the county did manage to see some beneficial rainfall returning this portion of the county back to Moderate Drought (D1).

Deaf Smith was receiving some good rain in July improving drought conditions slightly prior to August. August was a different story with extreme drought conditions expanding from the south to the north. During the month, Hereford received a measly 0.18 inches of rain which increased the deficit by about 2.5 inches.  Almost all of the August rain events missed Deaf Smith and Randall Counties to the north and northwest. Conditions are so bad farmers are not going to be able to plant winter wheat.  About 16,200 acres of non-irrigated cotton crop as perished due to the drought. Corn has had a 10% yield reduction from last year due to the extreme dry conditions during pollination.

Donley County had only a small area of severe drought in the far south, going into August. By mid-August the whole south to southwest half of the county was seeing severe drought condtions.  Wides spread rain on August 29th brought some much needed moisture for the top soil. This allowed all areas in the county to improve to moderate drought (D1) conditions just before the month ended.

The northern half of Gray County started August out in Extreme Drought (D3), with a small area of Severe Drought (D2) separating the southern half which was in Moderate Drought (D1) in the beginning of the month.  Much of the county was still 1 to 2 inches below average for the month, even with some areas receiving up to 2 inches. Part of this 2 inches that fell, fell at the end of the month, allowing for the Extreme Drought to be reduced to Severe Drought. But the vast majority of the county still ended in the month in Extreme Drought.

The southern third of Hemphill County began the month in severe (D2) drought with less dire conditions across the north. In August,  slightly below average rainfall was received and enought to lead to removal of D2 drought conditions.  However, some moderate drought (D1) did persist across the south.

The far southeast corner of Hutchinson County began the month in severe (D2) to extreme (D3) drought. In August, 2.5 to 5 inches of rain fell which was near to slightly above normal for the month and this led to an end of the severe to extreme drought across the county, however some moderate drought (D1) did persist as annual deficits of around 8 inches or more remained.

The southern third of Roberts County began the month in severe (D2) to extreme (D3) drought with less dire conditions across the north. In August, near average rainfall of 2 to 4 inches led to an end of the severe to extreme drought across the county, however some moderate drought (D1) did persist.

An area of extreme drought (D3) existed in the northwest portion of the county with surrounding severe drought (D2) conditions surrounding at the beginning of the month. August did not bring very much rain, causing areas of severe drought to spread across the majority of the county by the 3rd week. Finally on the evening of August 29th a large line of storms moved through the combined Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles dropping any where between 1 and 2 inches for many areas. This one event dropped Wheeler County out of extreme and severe drought conditions as it resupplied some much needed soil moisture.

Randall County started the month out in widespread severe drought (D2) with a small area of extreme drought (D3) at the beginning of the month. Almost all of the rain events in August missed a good portion of the southern half of the county increasing the yearly deficit for precipitation. Canyon, TX and other areas of the county are around 6 to 12 inches below average year to date.  Top soil moisture is very poor with almost no grasses to be seen.  Hay prices in the TX PH were $10 to $20 higher per ton compared to the rest of the state. A lot of dry land crops were abandoned and non-irrigated crops did not grow. There was even a wildfire that burned just over 400 acres southeast of Buffalo Lake on August 11.

The Jackalope Fire began about ten miles north of Pampa Texas in Roberts|County around 1445CST. The wildfire began just east of Texas State Highway 70 in southwest Roberts County and was burning in a grass fuel type. The wildfire was being managed by the Texas A&M Forest Service in unified command with local fire department resources. The cause of the wildfire was determined to be mechanical from a roadside start. The wildfire resisted initial attack efforts and ultimately crossed the Farm to Market Road 283 impacting traffic due to fire activity and suppression efforts. Farm to Market Road 283 had to be closed around 1931CST due to fire operations. Multiple fire agencies and one private aircraft were called to assist with the control efforts of the fire leading to successful control of priority areas into the early morning hours of October 12. There were a total of sixty-five personnel fighting the fire. There were ten structures and two ranch compounds which were threatened, however no structures were lost during the initial operational period. The fire consumed eleven thousand five hundred and twenty acres which was measured with GPS mapping and  established dozer line construction was completed around the perimeter of the fire. There were no reports of any injuries, near misses or fatalities. The wildfire was contained approximately 1600CST on October 14, 2020.

The Texhoma Command Fire began about nine miles east southeast of Griggs Oklahoma  in Texas County around 2025CST. There were a total of five fire agencies that responded to the wildfire including the Guymon Fire Department, Texhoma VFD, Goodwell VFD, Yarborough VFD, and Stratford VFD with multiple brush units and tankers. The large grass fire burned in high CRP grassland and consumed an estimated three hundred acres. It was determined that the cause of the wildfire was from an incendiary device. There were no reports of any homes or other structures threatened, damaged or lost by the fire and there were also no reports of any injuries, near misses or fatalities. The wildfire was contained around 0000CST on October 12.
Stock trailer was rolled as a result of thunderstorm wind gust.

The western to southwest one third of the county was in severe drought (D2) through the entire month. There was a small portion of the southwest corner of the county that was in extreme drought (D3) going into the first of the month. This area of D3 quickly improved to D2 with beneficial rains that fell on the first of the month.  No other precipitation fell the rest of the month with D3 conditions creeping back into the southwest corner by the end of the month.  The county still remained in a 6 -12 rain deficit year to date by the end of the month.  Ranchers are still having to sell cattle or buy feed with range land grasses limited to non-existent.

Collingsworth County started out in with moderate drought (D1) in the west and northern part of the county, while almost half of the county in the east and southeast saw severe drought (D2) conditions. Thunderstorms on September 1st improved some of this area of severe drought but still left a good portion of the southeast corner in D2 status. The county remained in a 6 to 12 inch deficit year to date by the end of the month leaving some ranchers and farmers dealing with agricultural impacts such as shortage of range land grasses for cattle and dry soil conditions for crops.

Randall County was in extreme drought (D3) across the southern two thirds of the county going into September. The northern third was in severe drought conditions (D2). Conditions continued to worsen with less than a tenth of inch of rain on September 1st and no rain occurred for the rest of the month. By the end of September, a small sliver of the county in the far southwest degraded into exceptional drought (D4).  Conditions were so bad in September that farmers could not begin to plant winter wheat and were waiting for some soil moisture to return before planting could begin. Soil moisture was rated very poor to poor through the month of September. Some wells around canyon were reportedly going dry. Lake Tanglewood was reported to be at it's lowest level since the 2011-2012 drought and some boat lifts and piers were no longer usable. Ranchers are still having to sell cattle or buy feed with range land grasses non-existent. The county remained in a 6-12 rain deficit year to date by the end of the month.

Deaf Smith County was in extreme drought (D3) across the southern half of the county going into September. The northern half was in severe drought conditions (D2). Conditions continued to worsen with less than a tenth of inch of rain on September 1st and nothing the rest of the month. By the end of the month about a third of the county in the south degraded into exceptional drought (D4).  Conditions were so bad that farmers could not begin to plant winter wheat until soil moisture returned. Soil moisture was rated very poor to poor through the month of September. Ranchers are still having to sell cattle or buy feed with range land grasses almost non-existent. The county remained in a 6-12 rainfall deficit year to date by the end of the month.

Gray County started the month of September with a majority of the county in severe drought (D2). The exception to this was the far west and far southern part of the county that was only in moderate drought (D1). Gray County received a quarter to three quarters of an inch of rain on September 1st. This was only enough moisture to keep the county from degrading through the month as there was no other rainfall for the month. Condition were so bad that farmers could not begin to plant winter wheat until soil moisture returned. Soil moisture was rated poor to fair through the month of September. Ranchers are still having to sell cattle or buy feed with range land grasses limited. The county remained in a 6-12 year to date rainfall deficit by the end of the month.

Cimarron County continued to have an 8 to 12 inch rainfall deficit with the hardest hit area being the northwest half of the county. The county saw minimal rain, on the first of the month allowing for conditions to not deteriorate further, but amounts were not enough to improve conditions. Biggest impacts from the drought conditions all year thus far is no range land grasses for cattle. Farmers have been having to rely solely on irrigation depleting aquifers.

Beaver County received some beneficial rain from monsoonal moisture during the first of the month with the county already in moderate drought (D1). No more rainfall was received during the rest of the month and conditions started to deteriorate around the center of the county, with conditions worsening to severe drought (D2) and even extreme drought (D3). The rainfall deficit for the county was 6 to 12 inches year to date by the end of the month.

The Clawson Ranch Command wildfire began about four miles north of Hitchland Oklahoma in Texas County around 1321CST in CRP grass and open pasture land. The wildfire consumed a measured eight hundred and fifty-eight according to the Oklahoma Forestry Services and was caused by electrical arcing off power line. There was one home and one other structure that were threatened but were saved. There were no reports of any homes or other structures that were damaged or lost from the wildfire, however one engine was badly burned due to extreme wildfire behavior as the fire went under the engine. The engine was able to be driven away and parked. There were no reports of any injuries or fatalities. The Hardesty Volunteer Fire Department, the Guymon Fire Department along with the Hooker, Optima, Tyrone, Baker, Adams, Goodwell, Beaver, Turpin, Balko, Slapout, and Gruver, Texas fire departments responded to the wildfire. A Type 3 Strike team was called to assist with the wildfire out of Beaver County and the wildfire was finally contained around 2000CST.

Another round of snow on the evening of the 28th dropped an additional 4 to 8 inches where the higher amounts were across the central to eastern portions of the county. Overall snow totals ranged from 6 to 10 inches.

Multple periods of sleet and freezing rain led to light ice accumulations which caused hazardous driving conditions the morning of Monday, October 26th into Tuesday, October 27th. Five to seven inches of new snow fell on the evening of the 28th. The higher end of this new amount was in the far west and far eastern portions of the county.

A combination sleet and freezing rain led to light ice accumulations which caused hazardous driving conditions the morning of Monday, October 26th. Around 1 to 3 inches of snow fell going into the morning the 27th, then much more snow fell on the 28th. In the end, around 4 to 8 inches of snow fell across the county over the next two days with the higher amounts in the southeast half of the county.

A combination sleet and freezing rain led to light ice accumulations which caused hazardous driving conditions the morning of Monday, October 26th. One to two inches of sleet and snow mix fell early morning on the 27th. Estimated that .20 to .30 of ice accumulated with during the evening of the 27th on top of snow from that morning. Estimates of ice are based on surrounding observations with the higher amounts in the southeastern portion of the county. An additional 1 to 3 inches of snow fell on the evening of the 28th.

A combination sleet and snow pellets led to light accumulations which caused hazardous driving conditions the morning of Monday, October 26th. Three to eight inches fell across the county with the higher amounts in the far southern portion of the county over a two day period from October 27th to October 28th.

Light snow accumulations began early in the morning of October 26th, but the main snow events occurred over the next few days. Two day snow estimate of around 6 to 12 inches across the county from October 27th through the 28th. Higher amounts were located in the west to northwest corner of the county. First round of snow fell early morning on the 27th then more snow fell on the evening of the 28th.

Beaver County started out with a small area of extreme drought (D3). With no precipitation until the end of the month with an early winter storm came, severe drought (D2) conditions expand through the majority of the county before a winter storm late in the month improved conditions, leaving just a small area of D2 around the city of Beaver as the month closed.

A dry period through the month continued to make drought conditions worse. A good portion of the county started the month in severe drought (D2) and ended up in extreme drought (D3) by the end of the month. The southeast third of the county saw a little bit of an improvement from an early winter storm during the last few days of October. This improved the southeast from moderate drought (D1) to abnormally dry (D0).

Gray County started the month of October with roughtly 70 percent of the area experiencing severe drought (D2) conditions. With no precipitation within the first few weeks of the month the rest of the county slowly started to slip into severe drought, while a small area in the northwestern portion of the county started to see extreme drought (D3) conditions. An early winter storm  during the last week of the month dropped much needed moisture in the form of sleet, freezing rain, and snow. This improved the areas of severe drought to moderate drought, and the area of extreme drought to severe drought by the time the month came to an end.

Deaf Smith County continued to be one of the hardest hit places in the Texas Panhandle  for drought impacts. The county still remained in a 6 to 12 inch rainfall deficit year to date. Deaf Smith started out with a third of the southern portion of the county in exceptional drought (D4) conditions. The rest of the county was generally in extreme drought (D3) or severe drought (D2). An early winter storm dropped some moisture in the form of sleet, freezing rain, and snow during the last few days of the month. Though some areas of the county ended the month with some improvement, the majority of the county still remains in at the very least severe drought with some of the south still in extreme to exceptional drought.

Randall County started the month with two thirds of the area in extreme drought (D3) and the other third in severe drought (D2).   A very small portion of the southwestern corner of the county was in exceptional drought (D4) status.  An early winter storm in during the last few days of the month dropped much needed moisture in the form of sleet, freezing rain, and snow. The entire county saw at least a one category improvement from this event just before the month ended.

One fourth to one third of the county started out in severe drought (D2) conditions. By October 20th the entire county was classified in severe drought.  An early winter storm in during the last few days of the month dropped much needed moisture in the form of sleet, freezing rain, and snow.  Right as the month was ending, all areas in the county saw at least a one category improvement.

Collingsworth County started out the month with the far southeast corner in extreme drought (D3), with an area of severe drougth (D2) surrounding this area. The rest of the county was in moderate drought (D1) but gradually surcumbed to severe drought. The area of extreme drought grew northward along the eastern edge of the county as well.  An early winter storm during the last few days of the month dropped much needed moisture in the form of sleet, freezing rain, and snow. By the end of the month some of the northern and western edges of the county improved to moderate drought. The extreme drought in the county was isolated to the far southeastern corner of the county.

Almost the whole county started out the month in moderate drought (D1). A very dry start to the month gradually brought the southeast corner of the county into severe drought (D2) with the eastern, northern, and northwest corner degrading into D2 conditions as well by the 20th. An early winter storm during the last few days of the month provided much needed moisture in the form of sleet, freezing rain, and snow. This brought 99 percent of the county back into D1 status.

Hemphill County has been in a 4 to 12 inch deficit for rainfall this year and was in at least moderate drought (D1) for a much of the county going into October. By the 13th of the month 90 percent of the county went from being classified as moderate drought to being in severe drought (D2).  An early winter storm system hit the Panhandles on 26th through the 29th, improving the entire area of D2 back to D1.

Oldham County had seen quite the improvement in drought late summer into early fall, with almost all of the county dropping and staying in moderate drought (D1) at the most. Some of the western parts of the county had slipped into Severe Drought (D2) by the 13th.  In fact, a small portion in the far southwest portion of the county slipped into extreme drought (D3). This drought classification did not stay long, as an early winter storm provided some much needed ground moisture. By the 31st most of the county saw at least one categorical improvement in drought status.

Like much of the Texas Panhandle, Lipscomb County did not see any precipitation for several weeks since the beginning of September. The first few weeks of October were dry which led to a degradation in drought status on October 13th. Much of  Lipscomb was seeing severe drought (D2) conditions across the vast majority of the county after the 13th. An early winter storm late in the month improved conditions back to a moderate drought (D1) before the end of the month.

Potter County started the month out with maybe 2 to 3 percent of the county in severe drought (D2) to around 40 percent of the southern portion of the county in D2 by October 20th. This was due to the first few weeks of October being completely dry. This area of D2 did improve over the last week as a late winter event provided a decent amount of moisture as sleet, freezing rain, and snow over the span of 3 to 4 days.

Carson County started the month with the east to northeast half of the county in moderate drought. Lack of any moisture during the first 2 to 3 weeks of the month brought forth severe drought (D2) conditions to about two thirds of the area.  Conditions  did improve over the last week as a late winter event provided a decent amount of moisture as sleet, freezing rain, and snow over the span of 3 to 4 days.  Going into November, Carson County was only in abnormally dry to moderate drought conditions.

Donley County managed to remain in moderate drought (D1) through the first couple to three weeks of October. By October 20th conditions worsened with no rain to be had and much of the county fell into severe drought (D2).  An early winter storm in during the last few days of the month produced much needed moisture in the form of sleet, freezing rain, and snow. By the end of the month all of the county was back to moderate drought (D1).

The end of September was very dry going into the first few weeks of October. This lead to severe drought (D2) conditions spreading into the southeastern portion of the county by October 20th for mainly all areas south of the Canadian River. An early winter storm with freezing rain and snow during the last week of October improved conditions for these conditions to moderate drought (D1) just before the end of the month.

Roberts County was already seeing moderate drought conditions going into October. With the exception over a small sliver of severe drought (D2) up against Gray County. With the first few weeks of October being dry it did not take long for conditions to worsen with areas of D2 spreading northward.  By October 20th conditions worsened even more just north of Pampa, TX leaving a small area in extreme drought (D3) in southwest Roberts County. These drought conditions did lead to one wildfire that burned between 11000 and 12000 acres in Roberts County. An early winter storm in  late October dropped a decent amount of moisture improving conditions from  D2 to D1, as well as improving the area of D3 to D2 by November 1st.

The Shipp/Baca wildfire began about six miles northeast of Vega Texas in Oldham County around 1652CST. The wildfire began on the Baca Ranch and consumed approximately three hundred acres. The wildfire was determined to have been caused by downed power lines. There were no homes or other structures that were damaged or lost from the wildfire. There were also no reports of any injuries or fatalities. The wildfire was contained around 1918CST and was brought under control around 1942CST. The Adrian Volunteer Fire Department and EMS, Boys Ranch Fire and Rescue, and the Wildorado Volunteer Fire Department responded to the wildfire along with Vega Fire and Rescue.

A swath of six to eight inches of snow fell across the county along a corridor extending from the southwest corner to northeast corner. The highest amounts occurred across the southwest corner of the county just north of Perryton, TX.

A combination sleet and freezing rain led to light ice accumulations which caused hazardous driving conditions the morning of Monday, October 26th. Isolated sleet accumulaitons just under 1/2 inch occurred in a narrow band across the county. Freezing rain created problems of downed trees and power lines across the county with ice accumulations ranging from 0.25 inches to 0.50 inches during the late hours of the 27th. Where the higher range of these amounts were located in the southern portion of the county adjacent to Gray County. An additional 4 to 6 inches of snow fell on the evening of the 28th with the higher amounts located across the central to northern portions of the county.

A combination sleet and freezing rain led to light ice accumulations which caused hazardous driving conditions the morning of Monday, October 26th. Isolated sleet accumulaitons just under 1/2 inch occurred in a narrow band across the county. During the evening of the 27th freezing rain and sleet fell across the county with ice accumulations of 0.25 to 0.3 inches accretions being measured across the southeast corner of the county. During the evening of the 28th another round of wintry precipitation dropped 4 to 8 inches of new wet and heavy snow accumulations across the county. The highest amounts of 6 to 8 inches were located along and just north of I-40. With ice accumulations already existing on trees and powerline the combination of wind gusts to 45 mph together with the new snow caused downed tree limbs and power lines in some areas of the county with scattered power outages. School and business delays an closures occurred at verious times throughout the multiple day event.

A combination sleet and freezing rain led to light ice accumulations which caused hazardous driving conditions the morning of Monday, October 26th. Additional impacts occurred from half an inch of sleet on the morning of the 27th. During the evening of the 27th the county saw several hours of freezing rain that lead to ice accumulations of half an inch to three quarters of and inch across the majority of the county. This higher amounts of ice were located east of Pampa. These ice totals lead to wide spread power outages and broken tree limbs. An additional 2 to 3 inches of snow fell on the evening of the 28th.

A combination sleet and freezing rain led to light ice accumulations which caused hazardous driving conditions the morning of Monday, October 26th. Isolated sleet accumulaitons just under 1/2 inch occurred in a narrow band across the county. Additional  sleet accumulations upwards of half an inch along with light freezing rain accumulations occurred on the morning of the 27th. Another freezing rain episode during the evening of the 27th lead to 0.25 to 0.30 inches of ice accumulation mainly in the far eastern zones of the county. This lead to broken tree limbs and power poles leading to power outages. One more round of winter weather dropped three to eight inches of snow on the evening of the 28th. The higher snow amounts of around 8 inches were mainly in the north central portion of the county.

A combination sleet and freezing rain led to light ice accumulations which caused hazardous driving conditions the morning of Monday, October 26th. Additional minor impacts from winter weather occurred on the morning of the 27th from 1 to 2 inches of a sleet/snow mix. During the evening of the 27th the county saw several hours of freezing rain leading to ice accumulations of 0.25 to 0.3 inches in the mainly in the northern and eastern portions of the county. On the night of the 28th an additional 5 to 6 inches of snow fell mainly in the northern half of the county leading to already covered tree limbs and power lines breaking knocking out power in portions of the area including south Amarillo.

A combination sleet and freezing rain led to light ice accumulations which caused hazardous driving conditions the morning of Monday, October 26th. Isolated sleet accumulations just under 1/2 inch occurred in a narrow band across the county. Additional winter weather impacts from upwards of half an inch of sleet accumulations occurred on the morning of the 27th. This lead to very poor driving conditions. On the evening of the 28th, heavy snow led to 4 to 6 inch accumulations. The highest accumulations occurred in the far northern portions of the county adjacent to Lipscomb County and included Canadian, TX.

A combination sleet and freezing rain led to light ice accumulations which caused hazardous driving conditions the morning of Monday, October 26th. Additional impacs occurred on the morning of the 27th with sleet accumulations exceeding half an inch. Freezing rain fell on the 27th with accumulations ranging from one quarter to one half inch of ice.

Much of northwest Cimarron County is still 8 to 12 inches below average year to date. The county has seen a little bit of precipitation mostly in snowfall but has remained in quite a large deficit. The northwestern portion of the county remains the most impacted with extreme drought conditions (D3). Through the first 3 weeks of November the southeastern half of the county remained below severe drought (D2).  Severe drought spread further southeast by week 3 leavin only a third of the county in the southeast in moderate drought to abnormally dry conditions.

Most of Beaver County remained in moderate drought with an isolated area of severe drought (D2) in the central part of the county going into the month of November. On November 24th a line of thunderstorms moved through the area bringing the monthly precipiation total to one half an inch to an inch across the county. This allowed for conditions to improve to a status of abnormally dry for the whole county. There still remains a 4 to 6 inch deficit in precipitation year to date.

Going into the month of November only a small area of severe drought (D2) existed in north to northwest Gray County. With an already 6 to 12 inch annual deficit that increased by up to an additional inch, around 90 percent of the county was included in severe drought category by the end of the month.

Deaf Smith County had seen some improvements during the last days of October. With November seeing a monthly defect of around half an inch of rain. Areas in the southern half of the county that were in extreme drought (D3) to exceptional drought (D4) saw small expansions by the third week of November. Much of the northern half to third of the county remained in severe drought (D2) by the end of the month. The county still remains in a 8 to 12 inch rainfall deficit year to date. Pasture and unirrigated crops remained in very poor condition.

Roughly 80 percent of Randall County started the month of November in Severe Drought (D2). Conditions quickly returned to extreme drought (D3) in the south to southwest portion of the county given little rainfall in November. The county remained in an 8 to 12 inch rainfall deficit year to date by the end of the month.

Going into the month of November one half to three quarters of Collingsworth County was at least in severe drought (D2) with a small portion of the southeast corner in extreme drought (D3). With an 8 to 12 inch rainfall deficit year to date increasing by one half an inch to an inch by late November, additional degradations occurred after the third week of the month. During the last week one quarter of the central to southeast was in extreme drought conditions, while severe drought had spread across almost the whole rest of the county.

Donley County spent the first half of the month in moderate drought (D1). During this time the already 6 to 10 inch defecit of rainfall year to date started to grow by half an inch to just over an inch. This was enough to plunge almost all of the county into severe drought (D2) conditions by the end of the month.

For the month of November Wheeler County saw a monthly deficit of one half an inch to an inch. This added to a 6 to 12 inch defecit year to date. The county started out in moderate drought (D1), but by the third week had degraded into severe drought conditions (D2) across the entire county.
Sheriff's office reported golf ball size hail with damage to vehicles.
Accumulating hail up to an inch or two deep was reported, with the largest size being one inch in diameter.
Light accumulation of hail reported to cover the ground.
Light accumulations of hail were reported to cover the ground.

The Eastern wildfire consumed 87 acres which was measured using GPS. The wildfire began between 58th Avenue and Horizon Road and between Eastern and Grand Streets. The Texas A&M Forest Service, Amarillo Fire Department, Randall County Fire Department, Palisades and Tanglewood Fire Departments responded to the wildfire. There was a report by the Incident Commander that 1 home, 2 barns/shops and 2 outbuildings were lost. It was reported that 6 barns/shops, 11 outbuildings and 15 homes were saved due to the diligent efforts of firefighters. There were no reports of any injuries or fatalities. The wildfire was contained around 1824cst. Crews were working to increase containment, improve existing lines, suppression and mop up of priority areas around homes. Focus remained on mopping up priority areas and improving containment lines for the remainder of the operational period. There were no fire control concerns going into the next operational period and the fire was monitored by local firefighters until there were no areas showing heat or smoke.

The 21 Command wildfire began around 1215CST about two miles west southwest of Goodwell Oklahoma in Texas County. The wildfire started just south of County Highway 51 and between County Roads 20 and 21. The wildfire consumed four hundred and eleven acres and was listed as suspicious and determined to have been caused by an incendiary device. The Texas County Sheriff's Office was investigating. The Union Pacific railroad line was damaged with four hundred an eighty ties burned. The railroad and U.S. Highway 54 was closed for nearly two hours. There was a report that four homes were threatened but were saved. There were no reports of any damages, injuries or fatalities. The Goodwell Volunteer Fire Department, the Guymon Fire Department, the Texhoma Volunteer Fire Department, the Hough Volunteer Fire Department the Yarbrough Volunteer Fire Department, the Hooker Volunteer Fire Department, and the Stratford Texas Volunteer Fire Department responded to the wildfire. Texas County tankers and maintainers also responded. The Oklahoma Forestry Services Task Force responded from Woodward Oklahoma. The wildfire was contained in roughly six hours or about 1830CST.
Some light accumulations of hail covered the ground.

The 1299 wildfire began about seven miles north of Lake Meredith near Farm to Market Road 1913 and Farm to Market Road 3395 in Hutchinson County Texas around 1130CST.  The wildfire consumed seven hundred and seven acres, There were no reports of any homes or other structures lost or damaged and there were also no reports of any injuries or fatalities. The Borger Fire Department responded to the wildfire which was brought under control around 1600CST.

Snow started to fall early morning, starting in the eastern portions of the county and spreading west and south as the upper level low pressure system intensified. The first major snow accumulation report came in around 530 PM CST on the 2nd of December. This was a report of 6 inches 3 miles south of Slapout. Around 8 PM the Beaver County EM relayed a report they received from a storm spotter that Gate had received 12 inches by this time. Around 7 AM the next morning a community volunteer used CoCoRaHS to report that 8 miles north of Floris had received 7 inches of snow with this report. In the end, the northeastern half of the county received 6 to 12 inches of snow while the southwest half of the county received 4 to 6 inches. With areas in the adjacent county in the Oklahoma Panhandle, to the west, also receiving upwards of 5 inches of snow.

Snow began the evening of the 12th and ended on the morning of the 13th. The heaviest snow fall fell between midnight and 6 AM. Among the 5 to 8 inches that fell in the county, the higher amounts were in the northeastern portion of the county up against Kansas with an area of lighter amounts in central portions of the county before going back up to around 6 inches again in the southwest corner of the county.

Snow began to fall as early as 4 PM on the 12th and ended around 6 AM on the 13th. The heaviest of the snow fell between midnight and 4 AM on the 13th. Around 5 to 7 inches of snow fell in the western third to half of the county while areas in the east only saw 2 to 5 inches of snow. A spotter and 2 CoCoRaHS volunteers reported at least 6 inches and up to 6.5 inches around 12 miles south of Kenton, 2 miles west of Wheeless and 4 miles north-northeast of Black Mesa Park during the morning of the 13th.

About two thirds of the northwest portion of Cimarron County remained in extreme drought (D3) or severe drought (D2) from the beginning of December to the very end of the month. With December's average rainfall being low, not much really change in way of degradations or improvement in drought status through the month.  Cimarron County, especially the northwestern half, has had one of the longest running periods in severe to extreme drought this past year. Rangeland conditions continue to be poor with very limited to non-existent rangeland grasses. The county remains 8 to 12 inches below normal going back 1 year.

The majority of the Gray County was in severe drought (D2) through the month of December. There were only slight improvements in the southwest and northern edges of the county in the latter half of the month. This was due to these areas receiving upwards of 4 inches of snow around the 13th and 14th in the southwest corner of the county. Also, another 3 to 4 inches of snow fell around Pampa on the 15th. The county rainfall and melted snow deficit remained 8 to 12 inches below normal going back 1 year.

Around 90 percent of Wheeler County began and ended December in severe drought (D2) conditions. This was despite receiving a couple of inches of snow during the middle of the month. The county rainfall (and melted snow) totals remained 8 to 12 inches below normal going back 1 year.

Around 90 percent of Deaf Smith County remained in at least severe drought (D2) through the month of December. About a quarter of the county in the southern most portions remained in exceptional drought (D4) with the rest of the southern half of the county in extreme drought (D3). Soil moisture continues to be very poor to poor with not much hope for any winter wheat crop. The county rainfall (and melted snow) totals remained 8 to 12 inches below normal going back 1 year.

The entirety of Collingsworth County was in at least severe drought (D2) through the entire month of December. There was a small portion of the southeast corner that remained in extreme drought (D3) through this time. The county rainfall total remained 8 to 12 inches below normal going back 1 year.

Donley County saw 90 to 95 percent of the county in severe drought (D2) at the beginning of December. Snow fall around the 13th helped to improved much of the northwest portion to moderate drought (D1) and those conditions remained through the end of the month. The county rainfall totals remained 8 to 12 inches below normal over the past year.

In the beginning of the month Armstrong County saw severe drought (D2) in the southeast corner of the county. About half way through the month of December conditions improved in the southeast while the northwest portion of the county saw degradation into severe drought conditions. The county remained 8 to 12 inches below normal going back 1 year.

Randall County continued to see severe drought (D2) in the northern portions and extreme drought (D3) in southern portions through the month of December. The county remained 8 to 12 inches below normal going back 1 year.

Snow started to begin in Beaver County around 6 PM the evening of the 12th and ended around 8 AM in the morning of the 13th. With this event overnight, snow reports did not come in until the morning hours around the time light snow was ending. It is estimated, by radar and the progression of the storm that 6 inches of snow had fallen by 5 AM with little accumulations falling there after. With 6 to 8 inches of snow falling across the county, the higher amounts were in the north up against Kansas with decreasing amounts going south towards the Texas Panhandle.

The Guymon Fire Department responded to the Mile 2 Road/Road U Command wildfire located about nine miles southwest of Eva Oklahoma in Texas County. The wildfire began just east of Mile 2 Road and south of County Road 49 in the northwest part of Texas County. Other fire departments which responded to the wildfire were from Goodwell, Texhoma, Yarbrough, and Hough along with units from Morton County Kansas. The wildfire started about 1434CST and consumed five hundred and sixty acres in a very short time. The cause of the wildfire was determined to have been from an incendiary device. There were no reports of injuries or fatalities and there were also no reports of any homes or other structures damaged, threatened, or destroyed. The wildfire was contained roughly around 1800CST.

First wind gust of 59 mph occurred at 1000 CST. Another wind gust of 72 MPH occurred at 1055 CST at the Hooker mesonet. Several other non-thunderstorm wind gusts were measured by the mesonets in Eva and Goodwell, as well as the ASOS in Guymon during this time period. The 72 mph gust was the highest measured by the Hooker mesonet.
A peak wind gust 60 mph was noted in this time frame at the Beaver mesonet. There were also several sustained wind speeds measuring 40 to 45 mph during this time period.
Sustained winds reached 40 mph around 1020CST with max sustained wind measuring at 45 mph during this time period as well. Winds eventually fell below 40 mph by 1125CST.

Mesonets located around Eva, Goodwell, and Hooker measured sustained winds between 40 and 48 mph for close to 2 hours. The ASOS located in Guymon, OK also measured sustained winds topping out at 48 mph around 1038CST.

Sustained winds reached 40 mph first around 10CST and peaked at 1033CST with the mesonet located at Lake McClellan measuring sustained winds around 49 mph. Winds were consistently sustained above 40 mph through about 1300CST with some measurements reaching 40 mph through about 1530CST.

Several wind gusts up to 59 mph were measured at several mesonet sites in the county as well as an AWOS in Pampa. These wind gusts all occurred within 2 hours between 1030CST and 1230CST. The last gust was measured by the Pampa AWOS at 1210CST.

The Pampa AWOS in far southwestern Roberts County measured sustained winds of 40 mph or greater for roughly 3 hours. The highest sustained winds were measured at 47 mph at 1115 AM CST. It is estimated that winds were this high else where in the county as well due to conditions this day and surrounding measurements across the combined OK and TX Panhandle.
The Pampa AWOS measured a wind gust of 58 mph around 1055CST.

The West Texas mesonet site located 7 miles east of Borger measured sustained winds greater than 40 mph for roughly 3 hours during the late morning and early afternoon of the 15th. The highest sustained speeds measured at 47 mph around 1313CST with winds falling below 40 mph sustained around 1350CST.
Not only were sustained winds greater than 40 mph, but the West Texas Mesonet located east of Borger measured a couple of wind gusts between 58 and 60 MPH.
The West Texas Mesonet located at the Palo Duro Reservoir measured gust of 58 mph two times at 1038CST and 1051CST on the morning of the 15th.
The West Texas Mesonet site located at Palo Duro Reservoir measured sustained winds over 40 mph for almost three hours. The highest sustained speeds measured was 50 mph at 1051CST.
The AWOS located in Perryton, TX measured sustained winds around 40 mph during the early afternoon hours of the 15th.

The West Texas Mesonet site located 6 miles east of Canadian measured sustained winds of 40 mph or greater for about 3 hours during the morning and early afternoon of the 15th. The highest sustained wind measured was 45 mph.
Sustained winds exceeded 40 mph for several hours. No damage was rpeorted.
Sustained winds over 40 mph were recorded at 3 different mesonets and one AWOS in the county during the late morning and early afternoon hours on Jan 30th.
Two mesonets in the county measured a couple of wind gusts up to 60 mph between 1125CST and 1330CST on the 30th of Jan 2021. The ASOS at Guymon also measured one wind gust of 58 mph  at 1248CST.
Three different West Texas Mesonets measured sustained winds between 40 and 43 mph for roughly 5 hours.
Two different mesonets in Gray County measured sustained winds between 40 and 46 mph from about 9CST and 1530CST.
The West Texas Mesonet site near Palo Duro Reservoir measured sustained winds between 40 and 50 mph between 1132CST and 1502CST. The peak sustained measured 50 mph was around 1343CST.
The West Texas Mesonet located near Palo Reservoir measured 60 mph wind gust on two separate occasions. The first was at 1340CST and the second was at 1414CST.
Sustained winds exceeded 40 mph for around one hour. No significant damage was reported.
The West Texas Mesonet site located near Stinnett measured sustained winds 40 mph and greater between 1108CST and 1504CST peaking at 48 mph sustained at 1230CST.
Maximum wind gust of 59 mph was recorded. No significant damage was reported.
The AWOS located in Dumas, TX measured sustained winds of 40 mph or greater for about an hour with the peak sustained of 47 mph at 1155CST. No damage was reported.
Maximum wind gust of 58 mph occurred, however no damage was reported.

The West Texas Mesonet site located 4 miles east of Vega, TX measured sustained winds of 40 mph or greater from about 725CST to 1030CST. Sustained winds peaked at 45 mph around 921CST. Significant damage was not reported.
Sustained winds exceeded 40 mph for around 2 hours. No damage was reported.
Sustained winds exceeded 40 mph for around 6 hours with a peak value exceeding 50 mph sustained. No significant damage was reported.

Cimarron County continued to see extreme (D3) to severe (D2) drought conditions in the northwest two thirds of the county going into January. Though the the northwest two thirds stayed in at least severe drought conditions, the far northwest third saw improvements with the extreme drought status being dropped by week two. This was due to Kenton, OK receiving about 88 percent of its January normal rainfall in the first two weeks, mainly the second week of the month.

About two thirds of the county was in severe drought (D2) conditions going through the first three weeks of the month. A significant rain event produced about three quarters of inch of rain on the 24th which lead to areas of D2 improving to moderate drought (D1).

About a third of Donley County in the east to southeast was in severe drought (D2) conditions through the first 2 to 3 weeks of the month. A significant rain event produced about three quarters of an inch on the 24th allowing for all D2 areas to improve to Moderate Drought (D1) going into the final week of the month.

Wheeler County continued with severe drought (D2) going into the month of January. Enough precipitation fell to help the western half of the county improve to moderate drought (D1). The eastern half of the county remained in D2 through the month.

The far southern portion of the county remained in exceptional (D4)  drought conditions through the whole month of January.  Further north in central portions extreme (D3) drought conditions continued with the northern half of the county seeing at least severe drought (D2) conditions. Areas around the county saw around 0.40 to 0.50 inches of precipitation during the month. Farmers in the area were looking at abandoning winter wheat for grain and turning towards using for silage. This did nothing to improve conditions in drought considering the County has been in a 10 to 12 inch deficit since January 2020.

Randall County continued to see severe (D2) to extreme (D3) drought conditions during the month of January 2021. Some places across the county saw around half an inch of precipitation during the month of January. However, this did not improve conditions, but only prevented further degradation. There was one wildfire in Randall County during the month due to the extremely dry conditions that combined with a high wind event.

Armstrong County continued to see severe (D2) drought conditions during the month in the west up against Randall County. Some severe drought conditions were present in the far southern part of the county through the first two weeks. Some of this area saw a one categorical improvement about half way through the month. Areas in central to eastern Armstrong County saw anywhere between three quarters to an inch of precipitation which is about normal for January to slightly above normal. This helped prevent any further degradation is drought conditions.

Collingsworth County remained in severe drought (D2) conditions through the first three weeks of Jan. There also was a small section in the far southeast corner of the county that was in extreme drought (D3). This all changed by the end of week three as areas around the county received close to three quarters of an inch of rainfall in one event on the 24th. The county was able to see one categorical improvement across the vast majority of the county going into the final week of the month.

The Beaver River Command wildfire began around 1421CST about four miles northwest of Guymon Oklahoma in Texas County. The wildfire consumed an estimated three hundred acres and was determined to have been caused by an incendiary device. There were no reports of any homes or other structures lost, damaged or threatened and no evacuations occurred. There were also no reports of any injuries or fatalities. This was a large grass fire, threatening the north city limits and residential area of Guymon. The Guymon, Hooker, Goodwell, Texhoma, Hardesty, Optima, Hough, and Yarbrough fire departments responded to the wildfire. The wildfire was contained around 2200CST.

Hartley County has been seeing abnormally dry (D0) to moderate drought (D1) conditions through the winter months. Minimal precipitation even during the 'drier months' of winter the southwest third of the county slipped back into severe drought (D2) conditions. Hartley County has not seen any areas in D2 since the end of October 2020.

After seeing a little improvement in drought conditions through the month of January, a good majority of the county slipped back into Severe Drought (D2) conditions just after the first week of February.

About a third of the county in the east to northeast portion remained in severe drought (D2) conditions through the month of February.  Some snow fell during the month but water content was minimal and the county saw no changes in drought through the month. Portions of the county remaind in a 6 to 12 inch deficit going back to February of last year.

Deaf Smith County remained one of the hardest hit counties in drought in the Texas Panhandle. The southern half of the county remained in extreme drought (D3) to exceptional drought (D4), with the majority of the northern county in at least severe drought (D2). Soil moisture continued to remain very poor to poor. Some snow in the middle of the month brought minimal amount of moisture during a historic cold event. Winter wheat and other cover crops were already looking grim and were expected to only be harvested for silage and not grain. The county remained in a 10 to 12 inch deficit for rainfall going back to February 2020, with portions of the far southern county having upwards of a 16 inch deficit.

The southwest third of the county remained in extreme drought (D3) through the month of February, while the majority of the north to northeast remained in severe drought (D2). The county remains in a 6 to 12 inch rainfall deficit going back to February of 2020.

The western part of the county up against Randall County continued to deal with severe drought (D2) conditions through the month of February. Some snow fell during mid month but liquid precipitation remained well below normal for the month. Portions of the county remained in a 6 to 12 inch deficit going back to February of last year.

Cimarron County entered the month of February with the northwest half of the county remain in Severe Drought (D2) through the month. There was very little change on either improvement or degradation during the month of February 2021. An extreme cold weather event brought brought some relief from fire weather conditions during the month but also brought other challenges to agriculture. Portions of the county remain in a 6 to 12 inch deficit for rainfall going back to February of last year.
